There was an open window in his chamber and a burglar was searching his pockets. POSER.—An amusing story is told by a Scotch contemporary of the little daughter of a game- keeper who lives in one of the lodges at Keith Hall. her father was telling her mother about the ar- rangements' for the Duke of York's visit, and how the Duke would drive round by hi § lodge. Next morning the little girl asked her mother with an awe-stricken face, "I say, mammy, wull ye ha'e to open the gate for the Duke, or wull he flee owre't ?" THRICE DEAD.—After the battle of Custom., a soldier Supposed to have been killed was entered on the books 'of his company, "Died on the 24th of June," &c. A few days afterwards it turned out that he was still alive, and the honest quarter master made the following entry: "Died by mis- take." At length there, came a letter from the Ministry of War announcing the death of the man at the hospital, when the sergeant recorded the fact as follows: "Re-died by order of the Ministry." A SOLOMON AND HYPNOTISM.—A story is told of a judge who lately had the hypnotic plea raised before him by a burglar. The prisoner claimed that he did not know that he was " burgling " that he did it automatically and unconsciously, sender the direction of a hypnotist. The judge said w,suld give him the full benefit of the law, and /also of his hypnotic misfortune. He thereupon sentenced the man to five years' penal servitude, but told him he could, if he chose, send for the hypnotist, and have himself made unconscious for the entire t4rm of his imprisonment. THE FRENCHMAN AND THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE. —A Frenchman who was on a visit to this country was one day leaving a large London railway station on a journey. The station was under repairs, and some scaffolding had been erecteei for the purpose. As the train was leaving the station it was seen to pass very near one of the scaffolds and the porter shouted out as a warning, "Look out ! " The Frenchman at once popped out his head, which came in violent contact with the structure. When he had come to his senses, he said, "Oh, these Englismen are great fools ; they say 'Look out' when they mean Look in.' I never liked their language. Oh, my poor head ! div.head: GRottlig: DO air A. L'S PATTIZIT S E LE-RISING FLOUB ILLUSTRATED FASHIONS,
div.p: GRottlig: DO air A. L'S PATTIZIT S E LE-RISING FLOUB ILLUSTRATED FASHIONS,

The acme of good dressing lies in adapting one's attire to the need of the hour' and therein lies the why and whesefore of the long-continued popu- larity of the skirt and blouse costume for holiday. making. Six or eight blouses of varying degrees of simplicity and elaboration is a none too ample allowance for a summer otitfit, for their chief beauty lies in their perfect freshness and clean- liness. Of these two should be of Viyella, three of muslin or batiste, two of silk and lace, and the remaining one of silk or- satin trimmed with net or chiffon and of a sufficiently dressy descrip- tion to do duty for evening wear. By the aid of these and a navy blue serge or tweed skirt of good cut, and a couple of a more diaphanous and dressy character, a well-turned-out appearance can always be maintainell. = •

An outdoor wrap easily thrown on is always necessary when travelling, and is of infinite com- fort when visiting at the seaside or in the country, when a chill arises after sunset, and a muslin toilette does not afford sufficient warmth. There are many varieties of coats and cloaks approved of at present by Madame la Mode and her votaries, !And it remains only for the would-be purchaser to consider carefully what style is most likely to suit not only her figure and complexion, but likewise her circumstances. The smart coat sketched is of the semi-fitting kind, and is made of frieze of a rusty brown tint strapped with satin of a lighter tone. The belt, which is used to confine the coat to the figure when it is worn closed, is -of orange yellow leather, a colour which competes closely with

div.head: SMART COAT.
div.p: A SMART COAT.

emerald green among the most popular of leatkar belts. Another variety of coat which is fashion- able is the very loose Kimono shape, which is usually expressed in canvas, taffetas or cloth, .with • the popular wide-cuffed sleeves or sleeves of the angel order. These angel sleeves are practically a falling frill of accordion-pleated material, and being loose and easy have the advantage of not crushing the sleeves of the toilette worn under- neath. The smartest collars are either a Paiglom or in the triple-caped highwayman's style, whilst some of the latest models are altogether innocent of any collar at all.

The short riBite is another modish variety, ending a few inches below the waist with either a dolman-shaped or small bishops sleeve set into a narrow wristband. This kind of coat is ex- pressed fEr the most part in linen or white cloth, bat requires careful cutting to prove successful, and if well cut is decidedly smart. Another new form of cloak falls straight from a narrow collar piece cut away from the neck, the soft folds of the material falling in graceful lines to the hem of the skirt. The cloak is shaped to the figure by pores, strappings of satin or velvet, or insertions of coarse guipure lace concealing the seams.
The coat depicted is of taffetas trimmed with a lace collar of such depth as almost to Merit the name of cape. A char of chiffon and long

div.head: USEII7L WRAP.
div.p: A USEII7L WRAP.

depending lace ends further enhance the appehr. mace of this comfortable wrap, which can be used as a dust cloak if desired. The sleeves are of a very wide loose description. Some of the most practical varieties of capes and eleaks which have been introduced lately have these depending ends put to a good use, as these are so L....sacred as to allow of being twisted round the neck so as Cu arrord additional warmth, and prove very welcome and cosy vehen one is exposed to a cutting wind during a long drive or on the sea. A tassel finished off these long ends. Other outdoor wraps have a com- fortable hood, which can be easily pulled up over the head and hat should a sudden stormy burst of wind or rain be unexpectedly encountered. Fringe is much uscd as a trimming to the rougher kind of capes and coats, especially those of the plaid or tartan description. The finer cloths and light wraps are ornamented either by strappings of the the material itself, of silk or satin, or are trimmed with lace of a coarse description. Sometimes pleated sae coats are preferred, the pleats being confined at the waist by a satin ribbon band. Three-quarter Empire coats are also fashionable, while the military overcoat in cloth or serge has a vogue all its own.
The dainty hat illustrated is of drawn white tulle draped with lace, trimmed with a couple a ostrich plum( lug

div.p: A DAINTY HAT.

chapeau of this description is suitable for garden party wear or for the most dressy social functions. There are many of these drawn tulle hats to be seen, and they always look pretty, and are exceedingly becoming. Some are trimmed with feathers, as in this instance; others boast long, sweeping ospreys, while others again have their beauty enhanced by clusters of small flowers, such as banksia nines, the wild strawberry Hower, or delicate toned violets or forget-me-nots. Some have the brims lined with rose petals. The fashion this slimmer for fruity millinery has been and is unusually decided, and.in some instances reached a sicliculous -Point, as one^ could not avoid noticing a wonderful sioiiatity to a salad. Grapes and entrants are, however, pretty in their own way, and the lastnatned fruit in both white and red varieties is mach used and looks most effective. eowernm

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 5 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 5 1902
WOMEN'S CHAT.
and

Most people retain the impressions of childhood, the King's cruise round the coast must have walled to his Majesty many early memories. lie remembered his first visit to the Isle of Man when of tender years, and there is little doubt that his Majesty bass vivid recollec- tion of his first acquaintance with Balmoral That was on the Bth September, 1842, just fifty four years ago, when Queen Victoria and the Prince Consort took up their residence there, with their three eldest children— the Priosess Royal, the Prince of Wales (now King Edward VII), and Prince Alfred. The King can hardly fail to recall the hearty welcome which the people of the Preside Highlands gave the Royal visitors, and it is certain that Queen Victoria never forgot it. The Castle of Balmoral was then bat a small place, and it was not until two or three years afterwards that the present building was completed. The holiday season has been prolific in diessters, and, to the boating and bathing fatalities, is now added a daily list of motor car accidents. The facilities offered to women and g'rls for learning to swirnotheuld certainly be taken advantage of wherever possible, but it should never be forgotten that a knowledge of swimming in- duces many people to take risks,which the non swimmer avoids, and women especially should be 'careful in not I over-rating their strength and powers of endurance. This is a fruitful source of disaster to bathers, whilst sheer recklessness accounts for most of the boating and motor car accidents. It was shown at the inquiry into the death el Ms and Mrs Fair that their motor was travelling at over ninety miles an hour, at the time of the accident. To many people it is incredible that any machine could travel on the highway at douLlethe speed of express trains, but such appears to be the case, and whilst people are allowed to indulge in the " speed mania "it is not surprising that accidents are of daily occurrence. The Alps appear to have claimed this season a full tale of victims, and there has been a good deal of discussion respecting the causes of so many deaths. No doubt one of the chief of these causes is the recklessness of 'tt'unexperieneed climbers, who attempt the ascent of difficult mountains without the assistance of guides. Another fruitful cause of accidents is the engagements of "guides" wbo are altogether incompet- ent. Judging from the qUalifications of some of these men it does not appear to be very difficult to obtain a certificate as a guide, and in this, as in all other depart- ments of life, there are men vibe talk plausibly of their own ability, bet are utterly independab.e. The man who employe such a one always loses something, and in the Alps he sometimes loses his life. The shop windows, as well as the country side, begin to show unmistakable signs of sutumn,and this means a general overhauling of frocks before we deside what fresh purchases are necessary for autumn wear. The wise amongst us who manage to pick up cheap rem- nants ef dress materials at the sales,are already provided for in some measure, and it is only by looking ahead that those with small means can hope to dress well. Tweeds, friezes, and serges are the principal materials for thick oestumee, and some women have scarcely bees able te diseard cloth dresses since last winter. A few have shivered in the cold in heroic endeavours to wear out their ;diaphanous toilettes, but not many bave suc- ceeded, aid summer frocks and hats may now be bad almost for the asking. The well.dreesed wonsan,how- ever, must always be prepared for the exigencies of the weather, and the rapidly ihortening days suggest that it is time to put the wardrobe in order for the change of seasons. There is almost a craze for Irish lace in America this year, and the makers should greatly benefit from the large demand for their exquisite productions. Scarcely any real lace is made in the United States. It is nearly all imported from Europe, and with the heavy cisterns duty, it is very dear. This however, is rather to the liking of leading American women, to whom money is no object, and who,when they come to Europe, are able to indulge in large and costly purchases. Some bays appeared this season in costumes composed entirely of Irish lace, and the late Mrs Fair, who was the sister-in- law of Mrs Vanderbilt, was wearing such a drese when she was killed with her husband in the smash up of their moter car.

Jewellery is not nearly so muds overworn as formerly, and well dressed women only don a little, and that is the best of its kind. The long chain with its weird coilection of curiositiee has long since disappeared and in its place only a thin gold neclechoin with a simple pendant is worn. The looped ;tortoise shell hairpins. now so popular,are being set with diamonds, real and unreal, but as they become more common, Society folk will in all probability discard this ornamentation for the hair. Pearls are as much in-vogue as ever,especially for earrings. Emeralds are also very popular. There does not however appear to be any particular novelty in what is called lucky jewellery, but no doubt it will not be long before some one succeeds in introducing a new fortune bearing charm• MADGE'

div.p: ALLEGED Al TEMPTED MURDER OF A PENKETH WOMAN

A body found in the Ship Canal; at -Cadishrad, on Saturday, was onlMonday identified as that of John Rost. On Monday/week the wife if Ross formerly or Peaketh was found lying seriouely injured is the bed- room if her homelliThe bed upon 'bleb she was lying was saturated with blood, and the twosomes head and body had been battered in a shocking manner. The woman was conveyed te the Salford Royal Hospital, where leer condition was found to be so serious that her depositions were rtaken. Up to Friday there were little hopes of her recovery, but she then began to show improvemeat, and she leas centinued to make steady progress. When the pollee searched the house they found a chair stained wit:l blood, and it was evident that thie article of furniture had caused the woman's injuries me husband had disappeared on the previous evening, and on leaving he told one of his three children that he was going to find a watery grave. From certain information receivedby the police they formed the opinion that Rosa bad attempted to murder his wife, and a description of the man was sent to all the police offices in the country. No tidings were received until Monday, however, when his dead body was identified as stated. The circumstances attending the death Allele formed the subject of an inquiry by Mr J F Price, the County Coroner, at Warn on Tuesday morning. A married woman named Jane Rutter, of HotherssP-street, Brough- ton, gave evidence of identification, in which she stated that the deceased, who was a wood turner, was last seen alive on the 24th of last month, about eight o'clook In the evening. He was a man of intemperate habits, and was always drunk on a Saturday. Witness was sure the body was that of Ross, for she identified him not only by his features, but by bis general- build and clothes.
The jury returned 9 verdict of "Feud drowned."

FUMBLEFIST,
BY GEOFFREY MORTIMER (Author of ." Tales from the Western Moors,' "Like Stars that Fall," &c., the.)
PART 1.-CHAPTER I.

The boy went with a lazy, slouching gait through Dipford Street, looking upon the ground, and whistling three bars of a peculiar metre hymn. He was a stranger unmistakably, for none of the inhabitants were at home in the busiest week of harvesting. The old foxhound, propped against the wall of the Crooked Billet Inn, merely blinked at the lad, knowing him for a " foreigner " ; and with a, languid snap at a fly that alighted on his nose, the one-time leader of the pack stretched the kink out of his back, and fell asleep again. Dip. lord village snuggles in a little basin made by barren hills, and the road to it mounts up and up to a jagged pile of granite, known as the Clatter- rocks. It is a lean and hungry land thereabouts, as bleak, they say, as Northley, "where the devil died o' cold." If it were not for the marshy bottoms, where the grass is rathe, no grazier in the parish could pay rent and tithe, and keep out of the grip of penury. At the four wind-beaten sycamores, just out of the village, the boy looked about him, still whist- ling, while he stood on a road-side boulder. From this perch he could see Smerdon Barton, a long, white farmhouse of one storey, built close to a steep sheltering bank of furze, with dwarfed Scotch firs here and there, and a few rowans on which the berries were already red. As he was scramb- ling over the stone wall, to make a direct cut to the farm, a man came down the road, carrying a cider firkin.
" Hoi, young yeller, there! Where be goen?" said Farmer Tozer. •
"Ain't this the way to Smerdon Barton ?" said the lad.
"It be and it baint, vor the matter o' that,'' replied the farmer. "'Tis a way vor them as has. business there—not otherwise. Who be ye?" "Joseph Lamb's my name. I'm going to work for Mr. Tozer." _ _

"Oh, zo you'ina the boy from Lunnon ? I'm John Tozer. I reckon you'm just come from the station? Lest zee, what is't they call the institooshun where you was eddicated ?" "'St. Margaret's Orphanage." " Ah, yes, I couldn't mind it, though I've got it writ down at home, zo as I mightn't vorget un. What age be ye ? " "Thirteen and five months." _

"Hum; it don't look to me as if they overfed 'e. You'll have to eat a dale o' bacon avore you'm half a man. I never did employ boys; but I've been indoosed to take 'e out o' charity. One boy half-a man, two boys half a boy, three boys no boy at-all. Did 'e ever hear that? One lad, zo be as he's etrang, can do the work of 'alf a man; two boys get at play, and don't equal one boy; and three boys is Old Nick when they'm together." Joseph Lamb grinned shyly. "Well, get along down to the house, and ask missis to give 'e a bite. Ain't ye got no corduroy breeches ?"

"No, sir, only these as I've got on." " Them's Sunday trousers; you'll tear 'em and muck 'm in half-a-day. And your boots ain't wuth tuppence for our work. What ye got in that bundle ? ' "A shirt and stockings, and a new Bible, sir." "Well, get along down. You zee yan scurry t' other zide o' the cleave?" said Farmer Tozer, point- ing to the valley. " Where, sir? " asked the boy. - " Where ! Straight as a gun barr'l avore your nose. I mean yon patch of rock amongst them oaks. You ain't able to understand our Devon. sheer talk, like all you up-country chaps. Come up athert there, where I'm a-pointin', and you'll vind zome of the hinds in a yield of oats. We'm stackin' in the barn, against drashin,' the day after to-morrow, and you can lend a hand when you'm had summut to eat. Understand me ?" "Yes, sir," said Josepit Lamb. There were six red yearlings in Lower Bradgates, and at the sight of a boy with a bundle, they came cantering across the field, with their tails held rigid and horizontal. Joseph gave one glance at the beasts, and, with a cry of fright, made a dash at a gap in the wattled fence, and plunged knee-deep into a mire on the other side. As he struggled out of the swamp on to firm ground, a girl's laugh rang from the court of the Barton. The Cockney orphan looked towards the house, his cheeks reddening, while a second peal greeted him.

"Oh, lor', mother !" cried the girl, "here's our new boy stugged a' ready in Lower Bradgates ! You shud a' zeen the sploush as he went in I " Mrs. Tozer came out of the pig-house, with an empty meal bowl in her hand. "Dear heart, is yan the new hind? What a comical little °Wick ! He's no more'n ten, vor certain. This way, boy, or you'll be stuvged agin —keep to your right. What did 'e come droo that gapway vor ? " "Please, ma'am, I thought the cows Would hurt me," said Joseph, blushing afresh at Sallie Tozer's giggles. "Cows ! Parcel o' gammon ! Be ye afeared o' them playful things?" said Mrs. Tozer. "I never was among 'em," explained the boy. "You'll have to get used to 'cm. They wudn't hurt a babby. Zo you'm Joseph Lamb ?" :4 Yes, ma'am, if you please. "Hem, Lamb by name and Lamb by natur', I'm thinkin'," muttered Mrs. Tozer, as she closed the pighouse door. " Zallie, where's your calf meal to? Come, slip about, my girl. Now, then, Joseph, come along o' me and have a bite in the kitchen." In three weeks everyone in Dipford parish, and a good number of folk in Clannock, knew that Farmer Tozer's boy from London was not worth the cost of his clothes and victuals. Some of the farmers chuckled over their whiskey at the Crooked Billet, and said that Tozer might have expected that such an unheard-of experiment would I.ie sure to prove a failure. . .

"I can't understand what can 'a' put zich a ridiclus notion into a sensible man's head," re- marked Butcher Mardon. "Wasn't as if he cudden vind a score o' handy chaps if he'd a mind." "There's no doubt but that this lad ain't got all his buttons," said Dick Truscott, the head-man on Smerdon Farm. "There 's a zort o' zilly look he's got, as shows it plain as the palm o' my hand. I'll zay this for un, though, he's a vine scholard for his ye'rs. If you was to pay me a hundred pounds I cudden indite a letter as he do. I can write, but 'tis the inditin' as bothers me. But, Lord love 'e, thikky boy can fill a. sheet o' paper wi' news when I he writes to his old mates in the Orphanage." " Ees, I dezzay the lad's got eddication," observed Michael Jarvis, the road-mender. "But • what's the good of it? Gi' me a boy as can use a pitchfork, and go dung-spreadin', or tend horses, and I don't care a darn vor his scholarship. 1 vind a scholard in bread-and-cheese, 1. wudn't. I've seen the. mischief o' learnin'. Why, talk about eddication who's goen to use the pick and shovel now edtheation's come in ? There's what / want to get at!" And so Joseph Lamb gained the character of a muddler and an incapable. He was so slow at learning how to put. the tackle on the horses, that Dick Truscott dubbed him " Fumblefist " ; and by this nickname he was called by everyone on the farm. Many lads would have been made miserable and spiteful by this derision, but Joseph was possessed of a stolid equanimity, and though he often shrank abashed from the jeers of the men, he went about whistling the three bars of his hymn, and was, upon the whole, happy at his work. He was summoned at five every morning, and, after a breakfast of soup and bread, he fed the three farm horses, and cleared the litter from the stables. Much of the roughest, uncleanest labour fell to his share, for he could do no work that called for skill and judgment. After one morning's ploughing, in which he failed to cut a single straight furrow, Joseph was set to furze cutting on the down, root pulling, and clearing pig-sties. One day Tozer sent the lad to Bradhembury market With three pigs. It was a wet, wild morn- mg, with scudding rain from the rolling inky clouds over Dartmoor, and Joseph was soaked to the skin before he reached the top of Barton Hill. He wore a sack over his shoulders, as a protection against the rain; and every rude gust sent the sobbled canvas over his head, while a jet from the brim of his hard felt hat poured down the nape of his neck. The pigs were young, active, and full of impish obstinacy. Every nye-way and gateway enticed them from the road, and when Joseph had turned two of them, the third would scramble up a bank, slip through the fence, and trot grunting across a field of swedes. Panting and stumbling among the roots, the boy would chase the runaway back to the road; but when he had turned it, the two other porkers could not be induced to go in the

direction or Bradhembury, and all three of them turned back for Smerdon Barton. These antics were repeated a dozen times in a mile ; the pigs seemed to thoroughly enjoy the sport ; and when Joseph sat down on the grass, and cried from sheer exasperation, the three surveyed him with an air of triumph in their cunning little eyes. "Oh, you nasty contrary brutes !" sobbed the boy, flinging his stick at them. "You mean to get me into trouble, do you? I wish you were cut up into sausage meat !" "Now what's to do?" said Farmer Tozer, jogging up on his stout, unclipped roan mare. "Dash the boy! Aren't you got no further than this? How am I goen to zell they pigs to-day? You ought to 'a' got 'em to market by HOW." "I can't get 'em along," said Joseph, tearfully. Then Farmer Tozer, forgetting that he was a Methodist and a Christian, dropped from his mare, and gave the boy a cut withhis stick, using phrases that are not becoming upon decent lips. "Go home, you young toad !" he roared. "Pack up your traps, and get ye back:to Lunnon, where they breeds vools and lunytics. Take the mare, and lead her back. Drat yer !" Joseph obeyed with a lump in his throat, and a smarting in the nether part of his body. "My Zallie's a better man than you be!" shouted the farmer. " Her 'ad 'a' got they pigs to market by now. Go on back to Lannon!" As he went down the hill with the mare, Joseph sniffed for a while, wiping his eyes with the wet sleeve of his ragged coat. But though his temper had been rudely ruffled by the pigs, he accepted the beating and the dismissal as part of the penalty of his existence. For an idea that he was of no use, and not wanted in the world, had been dinterl into his head when he awoke to the realisation of his peculiar origin. Some of the boys at the Orphanage had dim recollections of fathers and mothers and persons to whom they had belonged. But Joseph was without kith or kin. No one had ever spoken to him of his parents; and he was of the opinion that a freak of destiny had sent him into the world by some inexplicable and quite unusual process, and only permitted him to remain in it on sufferance. What was to become of him now? They had been glad to be rid of him from the Orphanage because there were two hundred boys there, and they ate a great deal, and food costs money. They would not take him in again. And without a farthing in hi pocket, how could he pay the railway fare to London? When he reached the barton, the boy met Dick in the court. _ _

"Well, Fumblefist," said Dick, "what be you back for? Ain't you zeed moister ? " "I couldn't get the pigs along, they was so stubborn," replied Joseph, "and Mr. Tozer told me to come home and pack up, and go back to London." "I thought that 'ud be the upshoot o' takin' you," said Dick. "Well, this is a bit of bad luck, zure enough! I reckon you didn't go stiddy enough with they pigs. What did e' want to scare 'em vor ? There's a nick in drivin' pigs, like everything else." "I went steady; it was the pigs that wouldn't go steady," explained Joseph. He stabled the mare and went into the house. Mrs. Tozer was in the dairy, making butter in a tub, manipulating the huge pat in the primitive mode of those parts. "Back a'ready !" she said. "What's to do ? " "Moister says I'm to go back to London. I ain't no use, ma'am." "It's always that way with Jan when he's upset," muttered Mrs. Tozer. "Go and get your dinner, Joe, and bide till moister comes home. There's a letter for you on the kitchen mantelshelf."

Joseph turned the letter over and over before opening the envelope. It was one of the few letters he had ever received, and he read the address with keen pride. It was not from a friend at the Orphanage, for the hand-writing was neat and straight. He tore open the envelope and took out a thin piece of paper, with 10/- printed upon it. The postal order was made payable to Joseph Lamb, but the sender had not signed his name. "Please, ma'am," said Joseph, when Mrs. Tozer came into the kitchen, "someone's sent me this." The farmer's wife put on her spectacles and took the order to the light. "Who in the world's sent it?" she said. "Well, you're a lucky one, Joe! Maybe the Lord's put it into someone's mind to send you this." "Maybe he has," answered Joseph. "Is it because I've tried not to tell lies, do you think, ma'am?" " I shouldn't wonder, Joe. I'll say that for 'e, that you'm truthful and honest, though you'm not what I should call bright and handy. Give the Lord thanks for that ten shillings, and don't you spend 'em on voolery and mischief." At five o'clock Tozer returned from the market. He was just brimful of kindness • for he had sold the pigs at a good price, and clinched the deal with !our glasses of gin hot. "Where's the boy to?" he said to his wife. " I told un to pack and go, but I didn't mane it this time. If zo be as he'll show a. bit more gumption, I'll gi' him another trial." So Joseph Lamb continued to chop mangels, iress the horses after ploughing, and do odd jobs, with a contented heart. On Sundays he went to the Methodist chapel, carrying his big, shiny, black Bible under his arm. Under the fly leaf of the volume he had written— " Joseph Lamb is icy name, England is my nation, Dipford is my dwelling-place, And Christ is my Salvation."

There was much discussion in the kitchen of evenings, concerning the anonymous postal order; and when another draft for a like amount arrived after the lapse of a month, Joseph began to receive some of the deference which the world affords to the moneyed. A boy of thirteen who possessed a whole sovereign was naturally envied by other lads. Dipford, like many other villages, boasted of a brass band. The chief euphonium player was Dick Truscott, and in his dinner hours and of nights Dick practised his notes in the barn. He had taught himself "The Death of Nelson" and a part of "Old Towles"; and Joseph used to sit on a sack of barley, listening to these airs with a huge admiration for the talent and patience which pro- duced them. One day the boy said: "I've a mind to learn music, so as I can play in the band. One doesn't need to be taught much, I s'pose ?" "Fay ! That's where yo tt make a mistake, Fumblefist," said Dick. "I learned to play in the band, though I picked up these here solos myself. It wants ear to play a wind instrument, and tkat's what you'm wantin . When I hears you whistlin' about the varm it zeta my teeth on edge, 'tis that flat and shrill-like."

But Joseph was not daunted. He was bent upon cultivating his-musical faculty, and to that end he purchased an old and much-battered cornet. Through the dark nights of winter, the owls that flitted silently in the light of the oil lamp in the stable window, heard strange and doleful sounds. "Poor Joe, he may try vor a thousand years, but he'll never learn a tune," said Dick to Farmer Tozer. "Howsoever, it keeps him out o' mischief." The persistence of the lad was pathetic, for he was as tune-deal as a savage. Yet for hour after hour, night after night, he sat on the corn-bin puffing his cheeks till they ached, without playing a single tune that could be recOgnieed. His horses munched on steadily; the rats that ran under the mangers became accustomed to the dismal tootling; the sleek, plump mice cleaned their faces at Joseph's feet, but none of them ever heard ten con- vcutive notes of music.

When the days .lengthened, and the harsh, dry winds drove the dust from the harrows, and set the yellow bells of the daffodils swaying in the vivid meads of Dipford Cleave, the passion of love arose in the bosom of Joseph Lamb. Sooner or later, Cupid's arrow pierces the village lad. Love and cider are the joys of the peasant's life, and love awakens early where other interests and desires are few. One noon an under-sized, red-haired girl, with crimson cheeks, knocked at the door of ,Smerdon Barton.

"It you plaise, ma'am," she piped, "do you want a maid?" • "Odds life ! You're not out o' short frodks, child," said Mrs. Tozer. "How old might they call 'ee ?" " Vourteen, if you plaise, ma'am; and they say I'm a good little girl to work." "Love us! You're fair spoken, anyhow," laughed Mrs. Tozer. " It does happen now that I need a maid." The girl's name was Naomi Widdecombe, and she came from Bradhembury to look for a place, She was one of a family of fourteen, all red-haired and red-checked. Mrs. Tozer engaged her at a shilling a week and her board. In three weeks, to the amusement of the folk at the farm' Joseph and Naomi were "keeping com- pany." On Sunday mornings they walked sedately to ehapel,_ hand-in-hand; and in the afternoons

tiley went bfrffs-nesting and Lent lily-picking together, with their arms around each other's necks. They were seen often at the dimming of spring days, roaming in Dipford Wood, with big bunches of primroses in their hands. Folk laughed as they passed by. A droller couple never went sweethearting. Joseph was growing out of his trousers, and his white socks showed above a pair of heavy hob-nailed boots. His face had always a bland, somewhat vacuous smile of contentment, while he held Naomi's hand and listened to her prattle. One evening the sweethearts were sitting on the bough of an oak, which a winter-storm had up- rooted. To keep their balance, they clasped each other around the waist, while the springy limb jogged them like a trotting pony ridden bare- backed. "Joe, they zay as you aint a proper lover," said Naomi, swinging her legs. "Why's that?" asked Joseph, in his gruff, good- humoured tone. _ _ .

"'Cos you don't know how to make love," she answered. "You never kiss me, nor call me dear. I reckon I shall vind a better young man than you.,, Joseph grinned bashfully. He had often thought that he ought to kiss Naomi on her pretty, pouting lips, but such a bold act needed courage. "I've a mind to kiss you now," he stuttered. "May I, Netomi ? " "No," she said, brusquely, as she withdrew her arm from his waist. _ . .

The boy's great grey eyes opened to their widest as he stared at her. Why was she so snappish all of a sudden? ft was his first experience of feminine perversity, and he sat pondering for several moments. .

" Well, I shall go home now," said Naomi, dropping to the ground and leaving Joseph joggling on the bough. "It's too cool to sit here any Longer.'' "Yes, 'tis rather cold,". remarked Joseph, following her. She walked quickly, a few yards in front of him. " Wh .t makes you in such a hurry?" asked Joseph. "Oh, I want to get back home," she replied, without turning her head. Joseph paced, looking on the ground, while he rubbed the back of his head with his hand. He was puzzled at Naomi's sudden unfriendliness, and he could think of no cause of offence on his side. But, in a flash, he discerned the cause, and obeying the first prompting of the male instinct of aggression, he caught Naomi from behind, bent back her little head, and kissed her valiantly on the cheek. "Don't!" she said, in a kind of half-smothered voice. But Joseph was re3klessly daring now, and his lips met Naomi's in a loud country smack. "Hi, fie there!" came a jovial tone from the lane. "I'll tell your mothers." The children looked up, with tingling cheeks, the colour of poppies. An old gentleman, very stout, and dressed in black, was standing by a gate. He had a pink, merry face, and short white whiskers. "Well, you've begun young," he chuckled. "Is that Master Joseph Lamb?" "Yes, sir," said Joseph, flushing again. "I want you, Joseph. I'm Mr. Tranter, of Newton Abbot, and I've come to tell you something to your advantage." The old gentleman chucked Naomi under the chin and put his band on Joseph's shoulder. Now, don't look frightened," be said. "I won't tell anyone what I've seen; I used to do it myself. You've come into money, Joseph Lamb— s tidy little fortune, too. What d'ye think of that, my lad ? " "Me, sir ? " stammered the boy. "Yes. Your father died a month ago in Gib- raltar, and he's left you. f,850." "I never had no father. It's some other Joseph Lamb," said Fumblefist, shaking his head. "Rubbish, stuff and gammon !" laughed the lawyer. "Your father went away when you were nine months old, and soon after that your mother put you into an or:shanage. She died when you were two years old; but you never saw her again because she went to America. Mr. Lamb, your father, kept a public-house in Gibraltar, and he has left this money to you. He has kept out of the way all these years." "Oh, jimmy!" gasped Joseph. "Am Ito have it all now, sir?" "No, you are to be paid twenty pounds of it. The rest is to be invested till you are eighteen. Come along up to the house, and write me a receipt for four five-pound notes. I want to catch the 8.30 train." Joseph was struck dumb with astonishment; he was too dazed to speak till they reached the barton. On the threshold he said: " 'Twas my father as sent them postal orders. Now I knows. I reckon I'm the richest Irian in Dipford parish." Farmer Tozer was in the kitchen when the lawyer and Joseph entered. "Bless me if it ain't Mr. Tranter !" he said. "It's a long time back along zince I rinned against you, air. Mother, get a jug o' zider for Lawyer Tranter, will 'e?" "I've come upon business with our young friend here," explained Mr. Trenton "Yes, sir, please," interposed Joseph, "the gentleman's brought me a fortin'." "A what!" cried Mrs. Tozer, at the door. "A vortune ?" cried the farmer. - Mr. Tranter handed some papers to Mr. Tozer. "Yes, that's so," he said. "Read for your- self." "Well, I'll be skinned ! Well, I'll be skinned!" repeated Tozer, looking at the documents. Fumblefist sat down on the settle, conscious of the gaze of Dick Truscott, who had been fetched from the shippons by Naomi. Everyone said: "Well, I never ! " and "Well done Joe ! " while the boy at smiling with a sense of the importance which Fate had suddenly bestowed upon him. Already he discovered that he was esteemed for his good fortune. Yes, he was the most distinguished personage in the parish (To be concluded.)
IHE TEA TRADE IN CHINA.
A Vanishing Industry.

I A report received at the Foreign Office from Foo- chow describes the tea trade in China as a vanishing industry. It states that the change which bas come over the tea trade, not of Foochow alone, but at other pro- ducing centres in China, and which is ruining what was once a flourishing industry, seems ascribable to several causes, not all within the power of the sufferert to remedy. Firstly, there is the indietputuable fact that the use of due care in the manipulation of the leaf when crowing, when being picked, and when being prepared for its transit over the sea is not exercised by the native grower. The means of ensuring all this have been repeatedly indicated to him, and put within his reach, with uo result, either owing to apathy, ignor- ance, or dogged conservatism. Ile has been in tarns implored, scolded, and lectured, but all to no purpose. Some years ago a circular wae issued by the Inspector General of the Customs warning tea growers that, citing to the superior methods prevailing , in India, the trade was slipping out 0 China's hands— bands that used to supply the world. It was recognised by Europeans interested in the industry that the lead taken by India and Ceylon had been secured by the sub- stitution of machinery for hand labour. Machinery was aecordingly imported. In some places more even than this was done in the effort to infuse new life into a moribund industry. While Formosa was still Chinese the Governor imported into the north of the island not only the rosohneery considered desirable, but even an expert from Assam. But neithet in Formosa nor in Foochow have these devises proved of any avail. To 1 the intelligent native they possibly appealed, but not to the fountain head—the grower and the picker, whose methods continued to be unscientific and primitive. His livelihood was obvieuely slipping from him, but the , prospect of even that catastrophe his bad no power to startle him from his invincible optimism. Secondly, there is the change which has come over the public taste in Europe. When China held the monopoly of tea pre ductioo, China tea was necessarily bought:. But when Alum and Ceylon entered into the competi- tion it was very soon apparent that the liking for their products was increasing rapidly, and China tea was in no long time hopelessly distanced. It is likely that, ei regards delicacy of flavour and aroma, the teas of China are still assured the suffrages of the cultivated le-ee Teas from the nearer East are admittedly coarser of e,ete, and contain a larger percentage of tannin, on , which aceount they are Condemned by medical men ae i , prejudicial to digestion. But they make an attractively 1 dark brew, and are eccnomical, in that a little of them I goes a long way. Thus they attract the sixpences of the many, sad it is on these sixpences that the merchant de- pends for his profits, not on the conservative and per- I baps more sensible half-crows of the cultivated few. I Thirdly, the trade in Indian and Ceylon teas has been fostered be judicious and persietent advertising, to which the Foochow merchants appear to have cot coo- descended to resort. Fourtiely, the trade is crushed by an exceseive export duty. Wien the duty on tea was firet made specific' it no doubt represented fairly en eugh the 5 per newt cid valorem 9%netiont d by treaty. The diminishing value of teas has, however, resulted in the export duty of to-day representing 41 instead of 5 pr cent.

Dr. Nilliams' Pink Pills Cure a Hopeless Consumptive;

One of her lungs, they said, was en- tirely gone. Treated at a pubFc institution in Leeds, she was pronounced to be dying. She could not walk upright, 'lnd was so pale, weak, and thin, that the doctor said it was useless to give her medicine. There is no doubt that she had bad the best medical treatment.
Mrs Guy was then induced to give her daughter Dr. Williams' pink pills. The first result noticed was

tsumptite, whose life was saved Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. that her appetite returued : she wes able to absorb food, and wanted more. ladeed, her appetite almost Caused alarm ; but her doctor saw she was going on well and had suddenly begun gaining strength. div.head: SEIZURE OF WARRINGTON GOODS IN AMERICA.
div.p: SEIZURE OF WARRINGTON GOODS IN AMERICA.

Mr. Fleming and his Fight with the Customs Authority. Mr E L Fleming, managing director of Meters Bishop and Compaav,uimited, borax manufacturers, Warrington, has arrived home again, fresh from his victory over the United States Customs Authorities. A reporter of the Examiner "sew Mr Fleming on Monday and obtained some further particulars , from him with reference to his recent acquittal in New York on a charge of evading the customs. In explaining the circumstances which led up to the ease, Mr Fleming stated that the United States Customs authorities seized a lot of 40 bags of wash- ing crystals, composed of borax and soda, which he had forwarded to New York by the White Star liner Tauric. The customs authorities contended that the bags contained fine borax which was liable to a tariff of five cents per pound, or £23 per ton, whereas washing crystals are only liable to a tariff ef ene-fifth of nne cent per pound. "I let it be known," he continued, "that I in- tended to fight the matter nut. I expected to be arrested as I walked down the gangway at New York, but there was no Government official there, There were simply some reporters, and I gave them any tale and let them know that I was going to the Fifth Avenue Hotel, so that if the Government wanted me they could get me straight away, On I the Monday morning I saw the United States Dis- trict Attorney in the Federal Buildings, New York, and I explained the cas- to him. At the first blush he did not think there was any ground for arrest. I said That is all very fine, but I want my goods.' He replied You cannot have the goods, yoa know I have not the power to let you hove them." Can I examine them? ' I said. He answered in the affirmative. I went to the stores and examined the goods that they had seized. I asked for a sample, but they said that Would be taking the goods away, and they could *tot allow it. I wanted a sample to get it tested by an American chemist.and after a good deal of bother and red-tape I got a sample by 'permission. I sought out the very beet chemist—Dr Waller, pro- fessor of Colombo University—and said 'I have a sample here. Would you test it for me and see if it Contains carbonate of soda? ' He did so, and gave rile a certificate of analysis that it did contain, as I Maintained it did, carbonate of soda. I thought that would settle the whole matter. I took the cer- tificate to the attorney, when he said • Now, Flem- ing, I shall have to arrest you.' I said. That is What I have come 3,000 miles for.' He said ' Well I Shall have to arrest you,' and I retorted • Well, I am here." He did not want exactly to be hard. and asked if I harl anyone to go bail. I said 'Net a soul. I am here all by myself, and if uncle Sam wants to take charce of me. well, he Will have to do so.' So he said 'Now, will you give Sae your word of honour that you will net leave New York city between now and Monday next? I Shall have you watched if you do. You can't get away.' I said 'No, certainly not. I have come to stop. lam not going away.' 'Be here on Monday Morning next. and you had better be represented by a lawyer,' he said. o I went on Monday morn- ing with my chemist, and he asked the chemist if be had tested the material I gave him. The chemist Said he had. He asked him if he took the material himself, and he said No.' The attorney perhaps thought that I had put some soda into the borax; and said ' Will you go to the stores and take a sample yourself under seal of the Government and send the result of your analysis to me direct ? ' Dr Waller said he would. When he did so, and it was found to be !the same they seemed to be more annoyed,for they then brother noceeded to put the m arrest into effect, came forward and wee bail for me until tll rn !' casecae on for trial." "And what was the charge preferred against you?" asked the reporter. "The charge was the falsification of invoices 'with reference to the coneignment question.nvoiTche es customs authorities contended that I was export. hg to America fine borax, whereas I held, proved in open court, that I was exporting wash- ing crystals. composed of borax and soda." "The trial toek place," continued Mr Fleming. "in the Federal Buildings. New York and lasted three days. The case excited considerable interest and Was fully reportedly' the press. The authorities stuck to their idea that it was fine borax, but a Simple demonstration in the Court Corroborated my statement. I showed the Court and everybody else the presence of carbonate of sodo. The material, wben tested, fizzed like champagne. The judge in summing up, said : I will, decide this case at once. I have followed it very carefully and con- sidered the evidence as it was offered. It does not seem to me that there is any criminal intention on the part of this gentleman. Re seems to have acted squarely and fairly, and I dismiss the com- plaint and discharge you." Questioned as to his opinion of the action of the rafted States Customs Authorities, Mr Fleming said he considered it was "playing the game very lew " when the Uaited States authorities took Criminal proceedings in what was purely a civil action. It was a very wicked thing to do. "You can imagine." be continued," what a commotion there Would be if an American manufacturer were placed Under arrest in England. Americans are getting Or ships and our railways and unless we stand np to them and fight them WS shall lose everything We have got. There is no disgrace in sticking up to a powerful Government, even if I had been defeated and locked up." Mr. Fleming concluded by saying that be con- Sidered the result ass defeat for the Borax Trust,He !!tends to continue exporting washing crystals. Mr Flouting has been warmly congratulated upon his Plucky fight.

div.head: MAYOR'S CORONATION MEDAL
div.p: THE MAYOR'S CORONATION MEDAL

The MAYOR read the following letter which he had received :—" Home Office. Whitehall,3oth August, 1902. Sir,—l have received the King's commands to transmit to you the accompanying medal, which his Majesty has been graciously pleased to canter upon you on the occa- sion of the Coronation of th,ir Majesties. I have to request that you will be good enough to send me an acknowledgment of the receipt of this decoration. I am, sir, your obedient servant, A. AKERS Donouts. The Mayor of the Birough of Warrington." He (the Mayor) had acknowledged the gift in the following terms :-- " Town Hall, Warrington September let. 1902. Sir.—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 30th ult. transmitting a medal which his Majeqty has been graciously pleased to comfier upon me as Mayor of the borough of Warrington em the occasion of their Majesties' Coronation, and I have the henour to ask you to convey my't humble thanks to nis M.joatv for the decoration.—l am air, your obedient servant, J. Cnartt- TON PARR. Mayor of Warrington. Tha Right Hon. A. Akers Doug.las, M.P., fllme Offiee." (Applause.) Tie (the Mayor) proposed to send the medal to the Museum for exhibition, and no doubt the people woul I he in- terested in the honour that had been dons to the borough. (Hear, hear.) The medal was handed round for inspection by the Council.

THE LATE MR S CHANDLET. A totter was received from Mrs Chandley thankie the Council for their expreasion of sympathy with her in the death of her husband, Mr Silvanus Claud ley, fern:pHs, an alderman of the boreinh. A TRIBUTE TO THE LATE MR E MILNER.

The MAYOR said it was with very great regret he bar) again to deplore the death of another worthy Warrington citizen in the person of air Edward Milner, J.P. It wag a long time niece Mr Milner hai ben an actual resident among them. bat they knew the deep Interest be took in the affairs of Warriegton in days gone by, and all that concerned its welfare and prosperity. He moved that the Council receive with regret the news of the death of Mr Milaer. and desired to express its siecere sympathy and condolence with the family in thGir bereavement. . .

The DEPUTY MAYOR, in seconding, said he would only be doing justice to the memory of the late Mr Milner by reminding the younger members of the Council—the older members needed no reminder—that he did some very good and able work in connection with Corporation matters, more especially as regarded the sanitary busi- ness of the municipality at a time when the sanitary reforms which had produced such powerful and good results in connection with the health of the town were certainly not as popular as they were to-day. He was one of the pioneers, together with the late Alderman Burgess,wbo did his best to bring about a healthier state ofpublic opinionland amore general and just appreciation of the necessity for the reforms which had produced so much good in recent times. Everything he had to do, both as a member of that Corporation and us. be Willy. • el, a corrrespondent for the People's College Committee, in which he took an active interest, he did with all lois might and with a sincerity of purpose that was the ad- miration of all his friends. His lose to the district with which he bad been associated of late years must be a considerable one, and those who had the pleasure of working with him in that town could appreciate the loss which the district had sustained. Alderman SUTTON said that as one ef the few members of the Council who sat in that chamber with the late Mr Edward Milner he would like to support the resolution, He could vouch for the fact that during the time that Mr Milner was a member of that Corporation he applied himself most assiduously to his duties. He (Alderman Sutton) supported everthing the Mayer and Alderman Roberts had said. He knew that Mr Milner worked hard, especially in connection with sanitary matters, and his opinions were always accepted with the greatest amount of respect. He knew, too, that when he left the town they all felt that they had suffered a very serious loss. ktlear, hear.) The resolution was passed. INSPECTOR SPINKS'S PENSION._

The following is a copy of a letter received by the Watch Committee :—" Whitehall, 12th August, Sir, In reply to your letter of the Bth ult respecting the perigion of Inspector Spinke, of the Warrington Borough Police Force, I am directed by the Secretary of State to refer you to the Home Office letter of the 10th March, 1899,t0 the Borough Treasurer of Warrington,and to say that notwithstanding the ease of Goodwin v the Corpor- ation of Sheffield, he does not propose to re-open the matter to which that lettor referred.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, CHARLES S. Mumma. The Town Clerk of Warrington." Tile committee expressed to the Chief Constable on behalf of the neembere of the Police Force their appreciation of the excellent services ren- dered by the men, and the admirable order maintained by them on Coronation Day. The MAYOR, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said it was extremely satisfactory that the Home Office had placed Inspector Spinke in the position the Council wished him to be placed in, and that the services of a worthy officer would be properly rewarded. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded, and the motion was agreed to. THE ADJUSTMENT OF FINANCIAL RELATIONS

div.head: PROPOSED HIGHER GRADE ELEHENTARY SCHOOL. PLANS TO BE PREPARED.
div.p: PROPOSED HIGHER GRADE ELEHENTARY SCHOOL. PLANS TO BE PREPARED.

At a meeting of the Museum Committee it was reported that the painting " Veeetian Water-Seller," by H Woods, R. 1., had been received. It was resolved that the report presented by the Secretary on the pro- posed higher grade school be adopted, and that Messrs W and S Owen he directed to prepare plans for the com- pletion of the Technical School buillines according to the scheme submitted to the Ceuncil• The report on the higher grade school by Mr Charles Madeley (secretary) appeared in last Saturday's " Examiner." The DEPUTY-MAYOR, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said there were, perhaps, two more im- portant minutes than usual. One was ie reference to the report of the secretary on the proposed higher grade school, and the other was to a certain extent the corol- lary, namely, the resolution that Messrs Owen prepare plans for the completion of the Technical School build- ings according to the scheme submitted to the Council. In reference to the report itself there were other mem- bers of the committee who were better able to speak with authority in regard to the proposale than himeelf. He was not a member of the tub-committee which had the special charge of technical instruction, but the minutes were always submitted to the parent oemmittee, the Museum Committee, for consideration and through that medium he, lite the other members, was kept more or less in touch with the proposals of the Technical Instruc- tion sub-Committee. The report which was a brief one, was so very explicit that it put the whole case for the proposed high grade elementary school as well as it could be put. There might be in the minds of some of the inemters of the Council the possibility of the school coining to some ex- tent into conflict with the present Grammar School or with the constitution later on of a secondary school as provided under the Education Bill now before Parlia- ment, but a little reflection would show that such a possibility was of the remotest character, in fact almost an impossibility. As far as the committee were con- cerned, they were of one tnind, and that was that they did not desire or intend to in any sense trespass upon the proper position of what would come more consist- ently under the denomination of a secondary school as intended by the present Education Bill. In reference to , the plan for the completion of the Technical school build- ings it PM not a 11610, thing The plane originally con- templated a complete scheme, but for reasons of peliey and necessity the Council had only been asked so far to sanction a portion of the scheme. In asking the Council to pass the resolution the committee were not in any sense prejudgiug the ultimate decision. If the plans were found to be too comprehensive or too napes- sive the Council would not be prejudiced in regard to its future action. The only expenses te which theylwould be committed would be the cost of the plans thetaaselvel. The committee had always submitted their propeeals in detail to the Council and they had never yet found any diffi- culty in carrying the Council with them in regard to any of their propoeals which the committee thought would commend themselves for their reasieneblenees and what they believed would be for the best intereste of the town. The committee would not (nine for any further expenditure of money unless they believed it to be absolutely necessary and desirable in the interest,' of the town and the future of Werringtoo. (Hear hear.) Couneillor Greening seconded the adoption of the minutes and the motion was carried wianimoualy. CEMETERY CeIefITTEE.

div.head: BEFORE BETTER THAN AFTER.
div.p: BEFORE BETTER THAN AFTER.

Francis 1., King of France. like most monarchs of his day and generation, was more concerned with his per- sonal pleasures than the well-being of his people, and passed the greater part of his time in jouste,tournaye, and revels, leaving questions of State to take care of themselves. The King had a Jester, a fellow of infinite wit and biting sarcasm, whose remarks were not always appreciated by the courtiers. This Jester one day with his pleasantry mortally offeeded a nobleman, who threatened to kill him,and of this the Jester complained to the King. " Fear not," said his majesty ; "If the Merquis kills you,l will have him hanged the day after." " I would greatly prefer," remarked the Jester, 0 that your majesty had him hanged the day before." The Jester was right. In most cases the day before is preferable to the day after. Had Mr George W Waldron,of t Dunetan's Crescent, Worcester, resoited to the use of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup when first attacked by indigestion, he would have been spared very much suffering. However, he came by the true remedy for that ailment at last, and writing on the 2nd of July,l9o2.thus records his experiences : " When be- tween twenty and twenty-six years of ae.e,it seemed as if I should develop into a chronic, dyspeptic. After eating, whatever the food at however slowly mesticated,l always felt unnaturally full and uncomfortable, this feeling being sometimes accompanied by a oatting pain across the chest. Heartburn was a constant source of torture to me. To these troubles must be added frequent bilious attacks, giddiness, and dull, persistent headache, so that, taken altogetaer, my life was far from being an enviable one. In the end Mother Seize.; Curative Syrup was brought to my notice, and happily I gave It '4: a trial. Three bottles of the bait-crown sin wrought a perfect cure, and I could after- wards partake freely of food that I had not dared to to touch for many a long day. I was so gratified that I have never since ceased to recommend it. I have spoken of it to scorer of my friends, and would on no account be without a bottle of it in the house. I have found it a true tonic, and have never yet taken a dose of it without feeling better and brighter in consequence. It seems to put new life and energy into one." There could only be one thing more satisf sctory than this statementlof Mr Waldron's,ani that is that his sufferings had been altogether averted—as they might have been. Yee, the day before is generally better than the day , after.

div.head: Pathetic Suicide of a Girl.
div.p: Pathetic Suicide of a Girl.

At Frodsham on Monday evening, the West Cheshire coroner, Mr Bate,held an inquest on Mary Alice Johneon,aged 14,wh0 committed suicide under remarkable circumstances. Deceased entered the service of Thomas Rigby, Bradley Farm, on the previous Monday as a domestic servant. On Friday she told Mrs Rigby she was sending a parcel con- taining some aprons to her aunt. Mrs Rigby examined the parcel, and found it contained eggs,a pinafore, and some shoes, which belonged to her. She told her husband, and he said he would go for the police. Deceased said "Do not go for the police." While Mr Rigby was changing his clothes in order to go for the police, the girl went out, and on Sunday her dead body was found in the river Weaver. Mrs Rigby said so far as they knew the girl had previously been honest.—The Coroner asked Mr Rigby if he did not think it rather harsh to tell a girl of that age that he was going for the police.—Witness did not reply.—The Foreman of the jury expressed the opinion that Mr Rigby had been harsh, and that it would have been better to have cautioned the girl instead of frightening her. —A verdict of "Suicide, but no evidence to show the state of the girl's mind," was returned. In referring to individual influence, the Chairman said be was afraid we did not exercise all the influence we might do for the good of our fellows. He believed in unity of action and said the trades unionists of this country were united not to injure the welfare of the community, but to promote it He would like to gee greater unity in the Church and more consistency in the lives of professing Christi-ins. Mr Power, of Manchester, delivered an impressive address. There were some, he said, who depreciated sentiment, but this world would be a very poor one to live in without it. He advised them to take Christ into their daily lives, and life would be all the sweeter to , them. Mr W H Walli:,gton led the singing in one of the hymns and also sang two solos with imich vignuT and feeling. div.head: Sermon to Young Men.
div.p: Sermon to Young Men.

The Rev John Tongs preached a snecial sermen to young men in Wyelife Church on Sunday evening, taking as his subject "The young man at Christ's feet." There was a large attendance, especially of young Peonle. The preaeher based his discourse on Mark 10, v 17. "There came one running and kneeled to Jesus end asked him, Good Maeter, what shall I do that may inherit eternal life ?" Evidently this young man, the preacher said, was of intelligent and even spiritual disposition. He had profited con- siderably by the religious training of his earlier days. As long as he could remember he had always striven to keep the commandments. He was a young man who had no past to deplore and therefore, as it might be thought, he was a young man who had no cause te be arxioue about the future. Before every common human standard of morality he was unimneachable, still he could not be content until he became certain about that grander and diviner Hereafter. In that respect he was an example to everyone, whether young or old. This young men's question " What shall I do to inherit eternal life ?" was surely the supremest question anyone acimi ask. All young men were intensely interested about their earthly future but had they ever given an hour's solid, Roller, serious thought to this matter of the eternal life ? Toe preacher proceeded to commend the courage of the rich young man in going direct to the Great teacher and becoming a humble questioner at the Master's feet. In allu line to the result of the interview and the subseqnent observation ot Christ " How hardly shell they which have riches enter into the Kingdom of Heaven." the preacher asked how could a man whose heart was set upon good be a millionaire in this world of millions of poor, helpless, downtrodden, despairing? Did they not often gee instances where as a man' e riches increased, his soul shrivelled ? Christ by his words meant to teach everybody the general truth that any- thing, it mattered not what, that would hinder complete obedience to God in personal life must be given up if eternal life was to be secured.

div.head: Golborne Street Baptist Church.
div.p: Golborne Street Baptist Church.

I The pastor of this church (Rev Herbert Dunnicol con- tinued his series ef talks on Sunday morning before a large congregation, the subject under discussion being "The doctrine e man." In the course of the sermon Mr Dunnico said that so far as the body of man Was con- cerned, theology had little to say except to note how truly both in structure and in material it was a part of the physical universe and that it was composed of the same matter as the planet upon which it lived. The Bible neither affirmed nor denied the evolutionary theory of creation and if Darwin's conclueioos were proved to be correct the value and authority of "The Book " would not be lessened. The Bible was net a text book lon science but a text book on religion. It did not claim to tell them "how the heavens go hut how to go to heaven." The spirit of man,the human ego,was incor- poreal and immaterial and they could not analyse it as they could the body. It manifested itself however in action,and observation of its action revealed three modes of activity which we termed intellect, sensibilities, and will. The moral faculty was sometimes looked upon al a fourth pewee but be (the preacher) fee various reasons preferred to look upon the moral nature as a resultant of the three essential powers already mentioned. The combination of these powers in a self-conscious unity constituted what was termed personality, and it was in the posses.. sloe of the powers that man differed from the animals below him and resembled God who created him. Man might resemble God.'in moral character, or he might not, but that likeness to God in whioh man WAS created could never be lost, except by annihilation or by the destruction of his personality. The preacher then spoke at some length upon the doctrine of immortality, and said that—Dr. Azar Beet notwithstanding—he was pre- pared to assert that man was by nature an immortal being. They must not be frightened by degrees sad diplomas. Upon matters like these khe spiritua man—and not the scholar and scientist—was the judge' Immortality did not neccessarily mean eternal existence but if a man denied eternal existence be must of neces- sity accept the doctrine of annihilation If they accepted the view that man was not naturally immortal they were compelled by sheer intellectual necessity to admit that the unconverted at any rate ended their existence in the grave and that punishment. judgment,and the potsibility of restoration were so far as they were con- cerned, out of the question.—ln the afternoon the monthly open meeting ef the adult Bible Mae, was held when there was an attendance of over 100. div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK ILLUSTRATED.
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK ILLUSTRATED.

This has been a gay and memorable week in the• proud old town of Preston. From north, south, east, and west, and from almost every clime, people have flocked to the ancient borough on the banks of the Ribble to celebrate the Guild Merchant, an old-time festival the like of which is unknown elsewhere in England. It is doubtful, indeed, if there is anything exactly like it anywhere in the world. Once every twenty years for seven centuries the quaint custom has been observed with due formality, and a regard for precedent almost as precise as in the case of a Coronation, and in this the Twentieth Century, the Guild is looked forward to with as keen an interest, and celebrated with as great a zest as it was in the days of Henry IL, by whom the first charter was granted to the Royal Borough. In olden times the members of the Guild Merchant were a business - like fraternity, and the privileges bestowed upon them by the series of Royal Charters were very

practical benefits, for which, doubtless, a good round sum had to be paid into the Royal coffers. The Charters were granted periodically and bore the signature of the Sovereign. The receipt of these Charters was a signal for much rejoicing. The principal streets were lavishly decorated, just as they have been this week, and there were gorgeous processions, as there are at the present time. The principal pageant, which has an educational object, is still the leading feature of the celebration, and as at bygone guilds it was no empty show designed for spectacular effect alone, but was intended to illustrate in concrete form the trades and industries of the town, and it was without question the most marvellous procession ever marshalled in this country. It is impossible in a brief note to even enumerate the various items of the week's programme, but the celebrations have included an agricultural show and a performance. of I,7ijak by the Preston Choral Society, assisted by the Halle orchestra. To be Guild Mayor of Preston is an honour well nigh as high and as much coveted as the Chief Magistracy of London, and on this occasion the Earl of Derby has the distinction of filling the office, and no more fitting choice could have been made by the Corporation when they elected him last November, for the famous Stanley family have been closely associated with Preston from time immemoriaL

There has passed away by the death of Mr. James Doel, one of the best known and most popular men in the theatrical world, for although the veteran actor retired from the stage more than a quarter-of-a-century ago, his name still continued to be associated with the profession he adorned for fifty-six years. The "Grand Old Man of the stage " he was called, and
, as such he will ever be remem-
bered, for he was
the wOrld's oldest actor. After he left the boards
his chief am-

birthday. He was

would reach the

LATE JAMES DOEL THE VETERAN ACTOR.
the event. Had he • lived until 1904 his am-

bition would have been realised, but alas! the curtain was rung down suddenly, and the genial old histrio died in his chair. Mr. Doel was never anything more than a useful general " character " actor, but he appeared with all the great actors of his day and played first gravedigger to the Hamlet of Maoready and Edmund Keen. As this was his favourite part, so was Shakespeate his favourite author; he was a diligent student of the Bard of Avon and appeared with distinction in many of his plays. He was a favourite with Sir Henry Irving and Sir Squire Bancroft, and, indeed, with every- body who knew him—and the names of his friends are legion.

It is said that explosives will have to be employed to blast the impregnable walls to pieces, but, although it will no doubt figure in history long after the imposing modern Sessions House which is to be built upon the famous and in- famous site ha di*appe irecl and been forgotten, we can see it splintered into fragments without emotion. After a very dull time the theatres are just beginning to re-open, and last Saturday night saw almOst the first important autumn production in Mr. George Alexander's re-appearance at the St. James's somewhat earlier than usual. He has selected Mr. Justin Huntley McCarthy's If I were King for his new season ; and it is one of those romantic picturesque " costume " melodramas to which he is so admirably suited. As in The Prisoner of Zelda, Mr. George Alexander finds himself King under unexpected circumstances, and does well in his unaccustomed rote. Mr. McCarthy has selected Paris under the cruel and superstitious Louis XI. as the scene, and the hero of the play, in real life a desperate and disgraceful scoundrel rather than a hero, is Francois Villon poet, patriot, revolutionary, ruffian and lady-killer. He is found boasting at the Fir Cone Tavern of his conquest of Katharine de Vaucelles, a great lady of the Court, Louis himself being present in disguise. Suddenly she breaks in in person, demanding that Francois shall prove his love to her by killing Thibaut d'Aussigay, the Grand Constable of Prance who is persecuting her unwarrantably. Thibaut enters, and Francois wounds him badly. He is arrested and drugged to sleep by Louis' orders; and, when he awakens, he finds himself in the Grand Constable's palace, addressed by all as "Monseigneur," for a week to be Grand Constable and rule France as he desired and then to be executed for his assault. This is Louis' cruel trick upon him, and the only condition which cau save him is the winning of Katharine's love. How -*Ss filibustering hero accomplishes this end of

Each boat is fitted with a torpedo tube at the forward end, and carries four Whitehead torpedoes. If these ungraceful-looking vessels are capable of doing all the damage it is claimed they can do, they will undoubtedly be a formidable engine of war—whether more so than their French and American cousins is a question many people would like to have answered. Grim old Newgate has been delivered into the hands of the housebreaker, and stone by stone, very slowly because of the granite-like solidity of the structure, the gloomy prison is disappearing from the heart of the great city upon whose fair, face it has been a foul fester for over a hundred and thirty years. Many a housebreaker of a different and less reputable type has Newgate held within its massive walls, but now, if a little play upon words may be allowed, the tables are turned, and the ring of the chisel and the clank of the crowbar are heard in and about the ancient pile. What would not scores of unhappy inmates 01 Newgate's dark, dank dungeons, have given in the stern days gone by for such unrestrained use of these implements! Thick and solidly built as are the plain grey walls, it would probably not have taken some of those desperate men long to hack and hew away through them to freedom But once the great iron-studded door had closed upon them and the heavy irons had been welded upon their limbs there was no escape from that terrible place of suffering until they were conveyed to the square opposite the gaol to be executed, or a more merciful death brought a welcome release. As a test of endurance and, tenacity of purpose Mr. Montague Holbein's great swim must be very nearly if not absolutely without parallel, and it is a subject of general regret that he should have so narrowly failed to achieve his object of swim- ming the Channel. Mr. Holbein was ip the water for over twenty-two hours, and covered, a distance of about tifty-three miles. When one considers fo- Mr. Holbein's feat is

MOItTAGUE HOLBEIN'S RECORD SWIM A CRART OE THE COURSE. nothing -Short of wonderful, and after such a magnificent display of constitutional vigour to have to give up in sight of the goal is hard luck indeed. However, the gallant swimmer, if dis- appointed, is by no Means dismayed, and he means to make a fourth attempt, starting this time from the English instead of the French coast. In this he will be following the example of Captain Webb, who swam the Channel in 1875. The ill- fated captain on that oc;asion covered 39-11 miles, and the swim occupied 2116,( I,3comurse,trwokhoilse oint Ntvhas e estimated that he made journey. Mr. Holbein calculates that he made something like 25,000 strokes to drive him those fifty-three miles. and it is said that he swam twice as fast as Captain Webb. Nautical men now seem to agree that the Dover side is the one from which to start, as the run of the water from the North Sea is swifter than the flow from the English Channel. Whether this is the case or not, Mr. Holbein has everybody's best wishes for success when he next essays the difficult crossing. Besides Mr. Holbein there are two other swimmers who aspire to hold a cross-Channel record—Mr. Frank Holmes, the Birmingham long distance amateur swimmer, and Mme. Isaceson, a Viennese lady, both of whom have made previous unsuccessful attempts to emulate Captain Webb, Mr. Holmes essaying the task no later than Mat week.

Commercial Scholarships in Cheshire. The Cuesuira °minty Council have for some ti been offa^ing commercial scholarships, but hither to tnuch to their disappointment, they have had no applications for them. Mr J W Litchfield,of Crewe,a tstadent at the Corporation Institute, has now wen Lite first commercial scholarship offered, value IX) yearly, for three years. Mr Litchfield also wins Lord Derby's scholarship, the blue ribbon of the aacashire anl Cheshire Union of Inetitates.
