SIIPIEMBRIL sth, 1902

WITH three years A The Trade Congress. war and reaction 101°12" it, the Trade 'Jai° Congress, which opened its sittings in London 00 Monday, has a sufficiently difficult situation t° face. Except that the very gravity of all the Cir.- ' cumstances has set in motion a robust moveleent of protest protest and revolt,the omens seem all able. The war has left its marks in every b 0 133,.e:, and only now that it in over have we full leiSti. to observe them. The returns of the numbers the unemployed are an unfailing index of the national prosperity, and this year they tell shrinking trade in almost every industry. Sl'r does this stand alone. Scarcely a trade but has t° report a fall of wages within the year, and in 50038 cases, especially in the North, the fall is very o°o- - Altogether, these statistics reVe situation worse for labour than in any year since 1895. But the decline in the income of tile working classes does not stand alone. Prices ha° risen more or less all round as a consequence of the war, and even rents have gone up in symPatb/ with bread and sugar, meat and tea. Taxatl°°,ll direct and indirect, is still more burdensome; in short, while the working man earns less than be did, his money will not go so far as it used. wonld be serious enough if the trade unio°s could face it with all their old confidence in tise power of organisation. But little by little, bit one legal decision after another, the right ° combination has been hedged and restricted' At the very moment when capital is combioieg more and more closely in amalgamations, syndi- cates, "combines," and trusts, it has become donbfr ful whether a trade union may take any aggressill action whatever in defence of its interests, witholl the risk of legal costs and penalties that vt0u1..." cripple it for ever. The Taff Vale Decision be' ' been ratified by the Unionist majority in Polio ment, and while it stands any Union which dere: in the last resort to organi se a strike, howevede sound its cause may be, may find itself =well 0 to indemnify the employer for his losses, and t stake even its benefit and provident funds on the issue of a costly lawsuit. The gravity of the danger is, perhaps, the nitt hopeful factor in the position. Organised 10°' is at last aroused to the risks it is running iu period of political reaction. In a moment of let; Ithe votes of the working classes put an enorni°o Unionist majority into power to conduct a Wao iwhich only Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S truculence 01.4 nevitable. It is quite another matter when 0101 'majority proceeds forthwith to destroy the 0013°0 Boards, to tax the public without representati°o for the benefit of the Church, to tamper with ITrade and tax the loaf, and, finally, to destroy tb° legal basis on which the workmen's right of cOre- bination rests. The revolt has begun in earnes% , and the Trade Congress has at last realised Oleo ts only security lies in capturing Parliament. 0.. 'has the money, it has the men, it has the orga°i'9o tion, and now the will is present also. AlreadY formidable election fund has been collected, °be with some confidence one may expect tbat t next General Election will result in the retnr° a.drong cohort of labour members. What the Conservatives will think of this pi° 0 merit we know already. Lord SALISBURY described trade unions as " cruel organisatiou; and Mr. CHAMERLAIN said in 1900 that a wer ing man in Parliament was "a fish out of wate'riii On the other hand, if Liberals are wise they wOl hail the new movement as one of the etrongelith all possible allies in the cause of progress. 8 no tact and sympathy on both sides there need be 5- cause for conflict. It would be a mistake, f°r e didate° ample, for Liberals to insist on Labour eau If, in toeing the party line in any formal way. 00 addition to their social programme, theY the opposed to a Jingo Imperialism, and favour d cause of justice and self-government for Irelear; they are better Liberals than many who abus I name.

THE Boer Generals are "Expropriation.' once more in London,this time engaged in some- thing of much greater moment than a mere visit of courtesy. On their meeting with Mr. BALFOUR and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will doubtless depend their whole attitude for the future. All parties seem to recognise that without their co-operation we can hardly expect the pacification of the new colonies to be more than temporary and super- ficial. But this is not to be had without condi- tions. The Boers, in General BOTHA'S words, are a ruined race," and everything turns on our good faith in carrying out the spirit of the treaty of peace, which assured them in the possession of their lands and promised them compensation for the wanton ravages of f arm-burning. Already even the " Times" has begun to warn us that the military are carrying out these arrangements on "the most strictly pettifogging lines." There is a risk of delay—delay " for years "—and "grave Injustice, and we are warned against a repetition of the stupid meanness which led to the Great Trek a

the original foundation of the Republics. But this is not the worst. Lard MILNER seems bent on taking advantage of the ruin of the burghers to drive large numbers of them from the land, and to plant British settlers in their place as CROMWELL did when he reconquered Ireland. He has actually asked for "general powers of ex- propriation," which will enable him to seize any NABOTH'S vineyard which a "loyalist " may covet, omd dispossess the Boer farmer who re- claimed it from the wilderness. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN approves the plan, and unless Liberals can make some effective protest there is a risk of an injustice and a folly so colossal that it must alien- ate the whole Dutch race in South Africa. First to ruin the Baers,and then ti) buy from them their devastated farms at a depreciated price, would be mean and unworthy. But when the element of force is introduced, and men already beggared are compelled to sell, meanness becomes a crime. The cant about inducing the two races to live amic- ably side by side becomes merely ridiculous when we:begin to plant British settlers by force on Beer farms, and then expect the evicted burgher to fraternise with the men :who dispossessed him. The result will be what it was in Ireland—an end- less racial conflict aggravated by agrarian strife.

Mr. Jerome K. Jerome's speech to the Liberals at Henley was anything but the "idle thoughts of an idle fellow." It contained thoughts and sentences which are good to hear and read in these days of half-hearted and cynical politics. On South Africa and its future government, on the Educa- tion Bill, on the Irish question, on the House of Lords, on foreign, colonial, and domestic policy, and, above all, on the duties and functions of the Liberal party towards itself and the nation, Mr. Jerome spoke brave and true words which Liberals should lay to heart. "The duty of the Liberal party," he said, "was not to follow public opinion, but to lead it. Liberalism that had not an idea of its own , Liberalism that was afraid to be Liberal for fear of offending the Tories who happen to call themselves Liberal; Liberalism that was second-hand Conservatism diluted with water--was not worth the trouble of crossing the road to vote for." Mr. Jerome is not an advocate of the "clean slate," which he would consign to "the political dustbin," but prefers the old Liberalism of Bright and Gladstone and Morley. That, he believes,is the Liberalism which won at Bury and Leeds, and so nearly won at Sevenoaks ; and that, we feel sure, is the Liberal- ism which will win at the nest General Election.

The Outlanders at Johannesburg are ungrateful dogs. We never expected them to be grateful to the people of this country, who have made so many sacrifices for them; but we did expect that they would show some gratitude to the man who, more than anyone else, got up and forced the war for their sakes. Au.i yet they have already begun to abuse Mr Chamberlain, because in the great speech that he made in the House of Commons towards the end of the session—his first speech after his accident—he hinted at the possi- bility of taxing the goldmines for the purpose of getting back some part of the cost of the war. The "Johannesburg Star" taunts him with "turning the fortunes of a colony to the base uses of an electioneering bait," and declares that the policy of taxing the goldmines is "taxation without representation with a vengeance." But the cruellest cut of all is its suggestion that "it might pay us to vote a million for electioneering in England, in order to protect ourselves from the consequences of Imperial finance or financial Imperialism." It is only a few weeks ago that those who in this country spoke of "financial Imperialism" were called "traitor" and "pro- Boers."

Lord Rosebery and the Liberal League are not to enjoy a monopoly of the "efficiency." cry. Ac- cording to Sir J Dickson- Poynder, M.P., the " ad- Tamed Tory democratic party," of which he considers himself a member, has for its policy "'to watch the great Home Departments—the Home Office, the Local Government Board, the Board of Trade, and the War Office—to see that their ad- ministration was kept up to date, and that the Ministers responsible for them vigilantly con- trolled the strings. It was also the policy of that party to look closely into our national expendi- ture, which was increasing by such leaps and bounds." We do not know who constitute that party, nor do we remember that Sir J Dickson-Poynder himself spoke or voted during the session for or against any proposal which could achieve any of the laudable objects enumerated by him. 0.1 his side of the House Mr Winston Churchill and Mr Bowles were the only advocates of retrenchment of expenditure or efficiency of administration, but even they rarely voted as they spoke. But if Sir J Dickson-Poynder is right in his statement that there are other Tories beside himself who hold these views, and are anxious to give effect to them, there is evidently an even stronger cleavage on the Government benches than on those of the Opposition' and the revolt against the Balfour-Cbamberlainregime may mani- fest itself in the • autumn session in an unexpected form. It behoves the Liberal party to be prepared for a possible defeat of the Government, and con- sequent appeal to the constituencies. ----- Mark Tapley, costermonger, of the North West of London, held his sports and gala on Monday That must be his name, says a, at Kensal Rise. correspondent of the "Manchester Guardian," for he managed to remain undamped in his spirits under the grievous visitations of the weather. The grand stand could not hold more than a quarter of the people who were there; but when it rained, which was pretty often up till three o'clock, the world without found all sorts of queer sheltering places, built up odd wigwams of 4 stray planks and canvas, and finally got under its carts. There were plenty of these drawn up round the edges of the athletic ground, for "your costermongers are very much carriage folk, and depend on no 'buses or trains. They drove up in every variety of market cart, ti e men smoking cigars, the women anxious about their " fevvers; and the nippers hanging on by their eyebrows to odd corners of the conveyance. It was a real costermonger crowd—tweed caps and amazing neckcloths and only an o 3casional collar, feathers and marvellous plushes ; and the population of Kensal Rise was even moved to cheers. As the crowd stood about round the track or gathered behind - the grand stand railings in -what it was pleased to call " the ring," there was always a cheerful ripple of amusement to answer the bray of the tethered donkey With a kind of professional interest. The sports were real eostermongers' sports too. There was a hand-barrow race, rattlingly noise, with " a pair

of trousers to measure" for second prize, and a Cardigan jacket for third—a most expert con- sideration of the street hawker's needs. Otherwise the prize list seemed to reveal an almost universal hankering for a marble timepiece or a "pair of handsome carvers in case." The mere outsider might frivolously wonder "In case of what?" But there was also a set of donkey harness for the "half -mile donkey-in barrow race," which had such entries as " Tired Tim "and " Who'd a fort it ?" and a mysterious animal named" K. Cid." A " box order for four" for a theatre was another remarkable prize; and sets of weights and scales brought the list back to a very practical channel. They were nearly all costers who ran, and cycled, and rode bare-back " wokes," and the latter event seemed, like the knights' battle in" Through the Looking-glass," to be chiefly designed for purposes of falling ofl. It was a cheerful afternoon, and it scored over the usual athletic meeting in having shooting galleries and cocoanut shies and other such delights to adjourn to when it was bored.

The report prepared by Mr. Madeley and issusd by the Museum and Technical Instruction Com- mittse will be read with keen interest by all who are directly or indirectly interested in the educe- tionalifacilities of the town of Warrington. It is a pleasing intimation that the committee has made arrangements to take over the management of the IPupil Teachers' Centre and distribute the classes II among the available rooms in the new Technical Institute. But the idea of providing a higher grade elementary school is of much greater im- portance, and the practical character of the report, I indicating clearly, as it does, the kind of school the committee have in view will give general satis faction. There is at present too great a gap between the elementary day school and the Technical Institute, and the new scheme appears to be one which will bridge the gap adequately and completely. Pupils. who have passed through the six or seven standards of the ordinary day school will, if the scheme is carrieA out, be afforded a splendid opportunity of following up and amplifying the instruction they 'have:already received until the Technical Institute, with its fine facilities for pursuing the higher ibranches of knowledge, becomes an easy and natural step. The course of instruction suggested ' as the curriculum for the new school is excellent In every respect, and there can be no doubt that it would obviate the existing educational deficiency. The question to be decided is the completion of the building scheme already appros ed by the Town Council. If they are willing to immediately countenance the additional expense the school could be ready for the autumn of 1903, and in this connection it will be well to bear in mind the fact that in the end there is more to be gained than lost by promptitude. The money will have to be spent some time and the sooner the better for the rising generation.

After beinavithin an ace of success Montagu Holbein has had once again to admit defeat in his attempt to emulate Captain Webb's cross-channel swim. This time he got within three-quarters of a mile of the shore in Dover Bay, but the ebbing tide was too much for him, and after struggling pluckily until he was almost at a standstill Holborn was lifted from th 3 water. The disappointment must have been bitter for he was "so near and yet so far." He had even swum the channel but the task was not complete until land was touched and the remorseless tide forbade this consummation of a great feat. Holbein has thesatisf action, however, lof having beaten several records for he was in the water over 22 hours and did rather more than 50 miles swimming in his zigzag course across the tides. Holbein is not the sort of man to give in even yet, and we fully believe he will try again to perform a task, which had it not already been accomplished, would seem impossible. Next time we hope, the gallant swimmer will try the con- trary route an I,start from Dover as did the famous Captain Webb. Mr Frank Holmes of Birming- ham, another aspirant for cross-channel honours, started from the English side on the day Holbein was finishing but was compelled to give up the attempt through sickness when about ten miles out.

Ix seems pretty clear now, allowing for the colouring of the facts by American journalists, that President Roosevelt escaped by the merest chance from the loss of his life. We are frequently asked to admire the facilities for quick locomo- tion in American cities, but sorre unpleaQant re- minders come that they have their disadvantages. There was no occasion, it is true, for the driver of the electric car to behave as he did; but we are reminded that in the narrow streets of our metropolis and old linglish towns such accidents are much more likely when we adopt rapid electric power for tramcars and omnibuses, and have motor-cars dashing about in addition. The lesson which is forced noon us is not that we are to be conservative and hesitating, bat that we must shew still more enterprise. We cannot afford the waste of time that occurs in gettiog to and from the suburbs of large cities,but we must meet the situation by widening our streets, and by severe punishments for those who then cause injury. The law of manslaughter is very little administered in this country; but it should, as we improve our thoroughfares, be easy to determine what is culpable and what is unavoid- able in this warfare of the streets. According to the letter of the law even pedestrians, who apologise for their presence in a roadway, have as much right to it as drivers of carriages, although the drivers of carriages are liable to penalties if they encroach on a tootway. This state of things is in theory not quite equitable, but in practice it is all in favour of the drivers. In London, of course, there should be shelving and rising roads at street crossings, to avoid the stop- page of vehicles from one or another side which occurs au the principal circuses. It is a matter which touches the provincial visitor quite as much as the resident, as he is concerned to make the most of his short time for business in town.

The Mayor of St Helens, Colonel W W Pilkington,was on Wednesday unanimously requested by the members Of the Town Council to continue In offict for another year. Colonel Pilkington was list November elec'ed from outside the Council, and he and Mrs Pilkington have discharged the duties of the office to the great pleasure and satistaction of the townspeople. Alderman J Porster presented the request in the Mvoc's parlour in presence of the members Of the Council, and said that they were delighted when he accepted the office, and also with the way in which he had carried out the duties.—Oolonel Pilkington, in reply, asked for time to consider the matter. div.head: RESCUE FROM DROWSING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: RESCUE FROM DROWSING AT RUNCORN.

Mr Daniel Edwards, a foreman at the Australian Alum Wore and a sergeant of the 2111 Cheshire Volunteers, has made a gallant rescue from drown- ing. He was returning home from his work along the banks of the Bridgewater Canal. Arriving at the crane he saw a child just d;sappearing beneath the surface of the water: Only the hands were visible. Divesting himself of his coat, and placing his watch on the ground, Mr Edwards dived into the canal and, securing the drowning boy, swam with him to the side. Restoratives were applied,and the youngster proved to be John Eastup, aged rive years. This is the third life Mr Edwards has been instrumental in saving.
_ EXCITING SCENE AT RUNCORN.-GALLANT RESCUE.

An exciting scene was witnessed on the Bridge- water Canal opposite Mr Nickson's building-yard at Runcorn on Thursday afternoon. Walter Clucas, one of Mr Nickson's apprenticas. aged 14 years,saw a boy in the water, and thought he was swimming, but quickly discovered to his alarm that the boy was evidently drowning. Without a moment's hesitation he ran from the workshop, and being a good swimmer, promptly jumped into the water. A few good strokes, and he reached the drowning boy, who clutched at Clucas in a fashion that his actions were much impeded. It was evident that the task was overtasking Clucas's strength, and Mr Edward Aston, foreman of the yard, although he could not swim, pushed a plank in the water as a float, and he and Clucas together got the boy to the side, lie was lifted out in an unconscious state, but several members of St John's Ambulance were on the scene,and their efforts were successful in bringing him round. He proved to be a boy named Newton, whose parents live in Duke- street, and he was taken home. Clucas was com- plimented on his brave deed. CHESHIRR COUNTY COUNCIL SCHOLARSHIPS.

The Technical Instruction Coramitve of the Cheshire County Council has made the following awards of scholarships :—Kvening Scholarships Instruction in Science or Technological Subjects, tenable for one winter season : John William Wiswall, Runcorn; James 11 Hill, Runcorn; i H Powell, Runcorn. The Technical Instruction Com- mittee have made grants for technical instruction purposes for the year 1902 3 to the following authorities, all having levied a p•.nny rate : Boroughs: Cougleton £206, Crewe £Bl2, Dukintield £365, Hyde £632 and Macclesfield £665. Urban Districts: Altrincham £324, Bollington £lOl, Hoy- lake and West Kirby £270, Middlewich £9O, North- wich £339, Runcorn £3lB, Sale £263, Wallasey £1,260, and Winsford £2OO. A resolution was also passed giving authority to the school boards of Braman, Congleton, Dukinfield, Disley, Stanley, Macclesfield. Moulton, Over, Runcorn and Staly- bridge to carry on for the period of one year from July 31, 1902, the work of their respective evening schools, and to apply to the maintenance of them such sums out of their school funds as may be necessary to maintain the same upon the scale of operations required. PICNIC TO CHESTER

The Victoria-road Board School nigger troupe held their annual outing to Chester on Saturday, and " one of them" sends us the following account of the outing :—" Leaving Runcorn by the 97 a.m. train, Chester was soon reached. Arriving at Chester, we entered the city by way of City-road and Foregate-street. Having inspected the Jubilee Clock Tower, the walls received our next attention. Proceeding by way of the cathedral, a short stay was made in order to visit the sacred edifice. After seeing the various objects of interest we again mounted the walls, and turning to the right we were soon before the Phcoaix Tower, better known as Charles's Tower, which is now used as a small museum. Leaving this historical tower we passed the northgate, and examined Morgan's Mount, Pemberton's Tower and the Water Tower. A gentle 'ascent brought us to the Watergate, and we nad 8 grand view of the famous Roodee. We now crossed over Grosvenor Bridge, with its magnificent stone arch, (largest ever erected). After crossing the road, we arrived at the Cagle of Chester, and visted the Barracks, and the famous Dee Mills. We next visited Haswells in Foregate- street, where dinner was provided and ample justice was done to the good things provided At the conclusion of dinner it was announced to us that Mr Littler, one of the members of the School Board, with his characteristic generosity had given us a donation, to be spent on ourselves. I would that he had been present when the announcement was made. file cheers from the boys nearly brought the building down. I take this opportunity of thanking Mr Littler for his kindness and good feel- ing towards us. Many of the boys were able to indulge a little more than they otherwise would have done.After:having satisfied the inner man,the party divided into two groups, one group visiting Eaton Hall, by way of Elccleston Ferry, whilst the other visited Pierrots &c. The two groups met again about 5.30 when we once more made an attack on the eatables of Foregate-street. After tea we examined the Rows, and the Market &c, after which we returned to the station having thoroughly enjoyed the outing. We were accompanied by the following teachers :—Mr Brown, Mr Parr and Miss Horsliela."

div.head: THEFT Or PRIZE POULTRY.
div.p: THEFT Or PRIZE POULTRY.

Mr Albert Widd, of Earlestown, breeder of the champion Leghorn fowls, was the victim of a cruel robbery on Friday. Someone broke into his farm at night and stole five of his famous Leghorn hens, one of which bred bim the National Cup winner at the last Crystal Palace Show, and the recent Royal Agricultural Show at Barrow. The loss to Mr Widd is very great, as this bird alone was Can- sidered by well-known judges in the fancy to be worth over .£5O, and was the finest stock hen ever bred. Thieves also entered the premises of Mr Rosette and Mr Haselden,of the same town,and took a large number ot fowls.

HORTICULTURE. --- Successful Show at Stockton Heath.

The members of the Stockton Heath Garden Society have cause for gratification in the complete success which attended the first an nual show of the Society which was held in the Church Room on Saturday after- noon. The exhibition of flowers and plants both by competitors and those who sent exhibits not for competi- tion was a highly creditable one. At this show, Mrs Crosfield, of Walton Lea ; Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr Henry Greenall, Mr Vere Davies of Darresfield • Dr Willett, Alderman Bolton, Mr R I Wynne-Jones, Mrj E Birtles and others contributed very much to the success of the show by sending very beautiful exhibits not for competition. Special notice should \be given of the exhibits of carnations by Mr R I Wynne-Jones and of sweet peas by Mr Onslow, gardener to Mr Vere Davies, which were greatly admired. A special certificate of merit was awarded for this exhibit.—The thanks of the Society are due to Mr Miller and Mr Lawie, who judged toe outdoor exhibits ; to Messrs William Kipps and James Lockhart, who were responsible for the show exhibits ; to Mrs A F Willett and her friends, who con- tributed to the pleasure of the visitors by a charming musical programme, and last, but not least, to tidies Edgerley, who always had a nice cup of tea for the officials, workers, and friends in the ante-room. The officials, who are to be complimented upon their efficient arrangements, were as follows :—President, Hey H V Pigot ; hon treasurer, Mr T R Westbnok ; lion secretary, Mr W H J Jenkins ; committee : Messrs A J W H Woodcock, S F Weeiel, Edward Vernon, J Ryan, A Broady, and J M )ore. The secretary, Mr i Jenkins, is deserving of special mention for his nains- taking and arduous efforts on the society's behalf. A special vote of thanks was accorded to the non-coin- petitors: The opening ceremony war performed by Mrs Henry Greeniili, of Hill Cliffe. She was accomoani-d on the Platform by the Mayoress of Warrington;Mrs J Charlton Parr), the President of the S-iciety (the Rev H V Pigot), Mrs Pigot, Mrs Eokersley and other friends.. Mrs Greenall, in a few happily chosen and felicitous words, expr3ssive of her Voil SVi4t3 for the future success and welfare of the society, declared the show open amid applaese. div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN.

Many Runcornians wilt hear with regret of the death of Mr William Haddock, of Brook-street, at the age of 64 The older inhabitams of the tawn will best remember the deceased as toe driver of Mr Jonathan Wilsoa's 'bus which something like half a century ago plied between Runcorn and Warrington. At the ear:y age of nine years Mr Haddock was placed with a farmer at Aston, and passed shortly afterwards into the service of Mr Jonathan Wilson, ia whose employ be remained for something like 15 years, a trus:ed and valued ssrvant. At that time railways and loJomotives were tow and far between, and it WAS tae deceased's privilege to convey on his 'bus many who were then noted personages in the town. They included such men as Mr Philip Whiteway, Sir Richard Brooke, Barr, Mr. S. Beckett Chadwick, of Daresbury Hall, Messrs: John and William Brundrit,, Messrs Charles, Thomas, and John Flazlehurst, and the late and much respected Rev Cation Barclay. When the etage 'ous disappeared before the modern and more comfortable system of travelling Mr Haddock entered the service of Mr Joseph Davies, of The Highlands, Higher Runcorn coal and salt merchant, where he remainnd a devoted servant until Mr Davies left the town. Upon Mr Davies leaving Runcorn almost his last act was to personally recommend Mr Haddock to the notice of Mr William Hayes, at that time the largest merchant in the town, and through Mr Davies' personal influence with Mr Hayes the deceased Was enabled to enter this merchant's service. Some years ago the Salt Union combine Was formed, and Mr. Hayes' interests were merged into the 'combine's concern. It is a m-st noteworthy fact that although many old and valued servants were at this I time pensiened off Mr. Haddock's services were retained Iby the Salt Union Co. t represent their shipping interests at the docks, and he was in this firm's service I when death overtook him. In polities the deceased was a staunch Tory, whilst his religious views leaned towards the broad and Evangelical Church Dirty. For all classes of humanity who suffered poverty or distress he had a kindly word, and many acts of charity might 'be credited to him. He leaves an aged mother to mourn his lose.

The funeral took place on Wednesday of last week amids manifestations of 'tearer'. Prior to the cortege leaving the house the hymn " Jesu, lover of my soul ' was rendered. By special request of the deceased him- self no hearse oe mourning vehicles were engaged, it being the deceased's earnest wish that his remains might be carried to their last resting-place by his old friends, The bearers were :—William Langley (foreman Runcorn Docks), Thomas Edwards, James Millington, M Lacy, Thomas Sidley, William Brockley, William LambErt and Edward Boden, foreman Runcorn Laybye. The mourners included—Mrs Haddock (widow), Mr Peter Elawthorne (brother-in-law), Lencl7n ; Mr and Mrs Hollingsworth (brother-in-law and sister-in-law), High Legh ' • Mr and Mrs Gibbs (brother-in-law and sister-in- law), Mr George and Mrs Hollingsworth (nephew and niece), Mr Thomas Lawton (nephew), Ralph, Bernard, and Harold Gibbs (nephews), the Misses Clara, May, and Jessie Gibbs (nieces), Annie and Ellen Lawton (nieces), Mr William Shaw (missioner to the Seamen's Institute), besides a large number of friends. The Salt Union Company were represented by their Runcorn manager, Mr George Summerfieli The funeral service, which was a most impressive one, was colducted by the Rev W Scholes, who had attended the deceased during his long and trying illness.

div.head: SAVAGE ASSAULT IsbEAR HAYDOCK. Singular Case at Warrington.
div.p: SAVAGE ASSAULT IsbEAR HAYDOCK. Singular Case at Warrington.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Bernard MeDonnall. Edward McDermott, Andrew Fitzpatrick, Thomas Connor (farm labourers), and John Boyle (collier), all residing at Ashton, were charged with assaulting John Cawfield, a fireman at Evans's Colliery, Haydock, on Sunday evening. Complainant said the prisoners wero strangers to him. Be met them on Sunday night in a lonely road between Haydoch and Golborne as he was taking his sister-in-law part of the way home. Prisoners used disgraceful language towards his sister-in-law, and complainant told them they were beasts to come out with finch language. Be went on for about 50 yards when prisoner McDonnell ran after him and struck him. Complainant retaliated in self-defence, and then all the prisoners and another man rushed upon him They kicked him and beat him with a stick, and cc hen they bad finished with him left him on his knees and he was so sore that he could hardly get up. Connor remarked : " Don't touch the woman, and I think you have given him enough." McDonnall said : " Only for you, Connor, I would have given him a lot more." Cfmplainant did not know how he would have been left, but for Connor Prisoners ran across some fields, and complainant fol- lowed them with a lamp he borrowed from a cyclist,but could not find them. He believed a police-constable found some of them in a field. IN itness's ribs were crushed and had been bandaged by a doctor. Jane Ann Quinn, sister-in-law of complainant, gave corroborative evidence. She said she recognirid all the prisoners. In the struggle she was knocked down and her dress was torn. One of the men snatched at her watch guard and broke it. John Goueh and James Whitfiod spoke to heating cries of " Murder" and going for assistance. P.S. Young said he saw the prisoners leave a public. house in Gflborne on Sunday night shortly before ten o'clock.

Inspector Palmer said he was on duty at Ashton on Sunday night when he heard a woman shouting Murder." He me‘; complainant with his face covered with blood and in a very exhausted condition, and Caw- field made complaints about the prisoners. He also saw the witness Quinn, whose drees wee torn, part of her chain gone, and she was in a very exhaueted state. He afterwards saw Connor being brought to the Polioe Stetion. McDonnell and McDermott were found in a field hiding, and they were also taken into custody. Boyle was apprehended at his home. Boyle, Connor and Fitzpatrick gave evidence on oath, and denied taking part in the assault. Each prisoner was fined 20s and costs, or one month's mprislament.

div.head: RUNCOriN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCOriN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above authority was held on Thursday morning in the Council Cumber. Present :—Messrs R H Posnettt (in the chair), W Hand- ley, D Btsbrown, M Sweetman, J H Salkeld, T Jones, J Wilson, F Wiswall, E Imison ; with Messrs E Marshall (secretary), F A Lake (law clerk), J Wilding (secretary), and Dr McDougall (medical officer).
BIRTH AND DEATH BIATE.
The Medical Officer reported that for the last month the births numbered 44 and the deaths 29. the corresponding period las; year the numbers were 33 and 31 respectively.
INFANT MORTALITY.
The Health Committee recommended that a copy of the report submitted by the Medical Officer to the cam- mttee on infant mortility be forwarded to the County Council.
Mr Jones proposed and Me Salk?ld seconded that the minutes be confirmed.

Mr Ellison thought it would bs profitable for the Council and the public if Dt McDougall's report was read. Infant inquest cases revealed the fact that many mothers did not know bow t treat their children.
Mr Handley said that the doctor thought it advisable that the report should go in the first instance to the County Council, who might make observations on it and so the report would be published. _ .
Tbe minutes were confirmed. SEATS FJR THE PARK.

The Highways and Buildings' Committee recommended that six seats be provided and fixed on Runcorn Elia and Weston-road ; and that the market be closed each day at 6 p.m. from the lit 03tober to the 31st Makch except on Saturdays. The minute was confirmed on the motion of ALESIS Sweetman and flandley the latter drawing a:tention Co the forzt that the reason why they proposed closing the market during the winter months at 6p.m. was becauie no business was done and there was', l big wa,te of gas.

div.head: DEFACING MAGAZINES.
div.p: DEFACING MAGAZINES.

The Library Committee recommended that six hard- wood chairs be purchased for the r At:retie° department; that in consequence of certain MagaZ la.-!S and papers in Ihe reading room bong d faced by the public, a new I notice be printed and bung on the wall, warning readers lof the courqueoce of their actiens, and asking the fre- qUentors oT too reading rooms to assist ihe committee and librarian in Maintaining order and preventing any defacement ; and that the yearly 'wort already pub- lished in these colums be approved. Mr Bisbrowa moved the adogrAoa of the mintres, and said that the library was becoming one of the b?st used Institutions in the town. He wai sorry to sta'e tha% periodicals and magazines were being constantly defca:d and they had decided to avail themselves of the Libraries Act to prosecute such offenders. The minutes were approved. THE PICTURE GALLERY.

Mr Imis2n drew attention to the fact that Mr Me.adowerAt's photo had recently been received. It would not be inappropriate to mention that it was mainly through his exertions that the local authority was transferred from the old building iii the Town H.ll square to the present building. Mr Biebrown said he had been associated with Mr M?adowcroft for four years and had pleasure in endois- iog the eulogistic remarks made by Mr Imison.
THE JUBILEE OF THE AUTHORITY.

Mr Handful, pointed out that next mduth woald see the jubilee of the authority. It would be agreeable, he thought, if they were to recognise the anniversary in some special form. The first meeting was held on Monday in November 1852 and there was only one mem- ber of that authority now alive. He referred to Me John Simpson who was the returning officer at that time and who though absent now from the town was present every das in spirit. At that time he would only be thirty years of ago and was entrusted with the important duty of conducting the first election of com- missioners; Their oldest continuous memb r was Mr S Taylor and he thought he should be their guest or that occasion which should be a time when past and present members could unite. He proposed that a committee be formed consisting of ti e chairman and vice-chairman of the Council, the chairman of the Finance Cnmittee and himself to consider the matter.
Mr Wilson seconded End the motion ‘O4B appr3v6 3.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS. ---- Pickthall—McDonald.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS. ---- Pickthall—McDonald.

On Wednesday afternoon at St. Paurs Wosleyan Church a very pretty wedding was solemnizad, Ora con- tracting parties being Mr John T Prekthall and Miss Nellie McDonald. Both parties are exce ,dingly well known in the town, the bridegroom baying been con- nected with several offices of the Wesleyan body prior , to his removal to London, wh.wi be now holds a position ' as analytical chemist to Messrs Knight and Sons. The bride, too, has for many years been a teacher at the Granville Street Board School and, has been exceed- ingly popular. Fortunately the weather was in harmony with the event and all the circumstances conspired to render the auspicious occasion all that could be desired. Promptly at one o'cbsck the bride arrived leaning on the arm of her father, Mr. Henry McDonald of Manchester. She looked extremely pretty in a beautiful dress of white I Jdian silk trimmed with vslenciennes lace and insertion. She also wore • coronet of orange blossom and silk veil and wore a necklace of ' pearls the gift of the bridegroom. Toe bride carried a fine /Mower bouquet composed of arum lilies, anemones and maiden hair fern. The bridesmaids were Miss Emma McDonal I (sister of the bride), M 145 Eliza Ligtot- foot (cousin of the bridegroom), Miss Fisrrie Pickthall (sister of the bridegroom) and Miss Marjory Hammond (cousin of the bride.) The first, and second bridesmaids were costumed in a dress of green voile, trimmed with cream silk and wore applique picture hats trimmed with black velvet chiffon and point lace to match. They also wore small diamond brooches the rift of tle bride- groom. Miss Marjory and Miss Florrie Pickthall wore lovely white muslin frocks tricnrnA wicu valencienes lace and insertion wit, large liberty bats to match. They each also wore a n.eklace of pearls the gift of the bridegroom and carried baskets of yedow marguerites while the chief bridesmaids carried sbowct bouqura of maidenhair fern and arum lillies. The bridal party were met at the altar by the bridegroom and the best man was Mr Alfred Dodd. The Rev Alfred Wells officiated, a very impressive cere- mony being closed with" The Voice that breathed o'er Eden." Mr Pritchard presided at the organ and played several excellent selections ot bridal music while the guests were taking their seats, subsequently finishing with "The Bridal March "and the " Weddinz March." A reception was afterwards held at Mr Jenyons, Speak- man-street, uncle of me bride which was largely at- tended. The happy couple subiequencly left tor South- port, the bride's travelling dress being of brown mauve cloth trimmed with panne silk. The wedding; presents were numerous and costly.

Successful Exhibition at the Royal Show. At tile Royal Lancashire kgricultural Show at Preston, this week. The first prize, £5O, for the best arranged arable farm of 150 acres and upwards with at leaiit two-thirds of its area under rotation of cropping was awarded to Mr Joshua Ball, of Southworth Hall, near Warrington. In the horses class, Mr J Makeague, Newton-le-Willows was awarded sezond prize for brood mare with foal at foot and third prize for the foal in the lhackney section.—At a meeting of the Council of ' the So:iety, Mr John White (chairman) said that Manchester had held out every encouragement to induce the society to hold tbe show there next year and he therefore proposed that the invitation be accepted.—Mr W W B Halton seconded the:proposi- tion remarking that Manchester and the large towns surrounding it were deeply convinced of the importance of commerce and agriculture going hand in band.—The proposition was carried with enthusiasm —Lot I Derby, in calling for a vote of thanks to the local committee, testified to the magnificent response which had been made to the appeal for local subscriptions. These, be said, bad realised £2,2i5, as compared with £1,712 at Liver- ! pool, the previous record.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPoNDEDiII. The Council meeting on Thursday was of a short and business-like character. It is to be noted with satisfaction that rigorous action is ta be taken against any one found damaging the periodicals in the reading room. Some mischievous person or persons have actually disfigured some of the magazines in the most diqgusting manner. This can hardly be put down to infant precocity for in some cases toe work is that of an adult brain. Now that the dread penalties of the law are dangled before th ei r eyes the probability is they will desist from their evil doing

Another pleasing feature of the library minutes Was the satisfactory annual report contained in them of the progress of the library. Mrs Jones, the librarian, was deservedly complimented upon her share of the work and there is reason to believe that the library will be even more useful in the future than it has been in the past.

It will be noted that there ii a movement a-foot to organize a gathering of the past and present members of the Old Authority and the Urban Coun cil. If the committee do succeed in arranging such a meeting the result should be not only interesting but instructive.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

There was but a moderate attendance at Irwell- lane on Monday on the occasion of the first match of the season. This was probably due to the fact I that the time of starting was not convenient to the majority. The match was, on the whole, a good one. Both teams turned out at their full strength. Hunslet had the advantage of playing with tdeir backs to the sun during the first half, hut they did not make as much of it as they might have done. From first to last they were outclassed, the home team fairly making :rings round their adversaries. The score, fifteen paints CO five, fully represents the play. In every point Runcorn was superior. Some pretty and effective bouts between the horns rear guards were witnessed and it is evident that the team this season will require some beating when on form. At no portion of the game did Hunslet look dangerous and their three quarters showed but indiff -rent form compared with the sprinters in green. Natur- ally the greatest irrerest was centred in the opers- tion of the " new old rule" which abolishes the , kick out and re-eitabiishes the old scrum. On Monday it had the effect of making the game much more close than it would have been under the old rule. Houghton famous at his "finding touch "pro• pensities showed that he had lost none of his old cunning in screwing the leather. The new rule plays right into his hand, or foot, and should give the team an immense advantage. It cannot be gainsaid but the chances of the Linnets are of a very hopeful nature, this year indeed.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. Successful Education Experiment.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. Successful Education Experiment.

On Wednesday afternoon the Mayor of St. Helens (Colonel W W Pilkington) presided over the monthly meetiug. At the meeting of tte Gas and Lighting Com- mittee the Gas Engineer submitted an application from the Rainhill County Asylum, asking whether the Cor- poration would consent to supply the asylum with gas to the extent of between 2,000,000 an 1 3,000,000 cubic feet per annum, and if so upon wrist terms. It was ' resolved, as the supply will be taken within the borough, that the asylum be supplied upon the same terms as private consumers within the borougb, viz., 2s 31 per 1.000 cubic fe. The minutes were confirmed.

At the meeting of the Health Commit'ee, Dr O'Keeffe alleged that the Isolation Hospital waa n t properly ventilated, and that patients had contracted bronchitis and prieum-nia in consequence —Mr Alderman Forster said the ventilation was on the lines laid down by the Local Government Board, and was as goad as it could be.—The minutes were confirmed, Toe School Attendance Committee had before them a report from the Superintendent upon the recent census of school children in the borough. The total numbsr of children uneer fourteen years of age was 29,410. of whom 11.577 were under five years of age, and 17,833 between the ages of five and fourteen years. The total at the previous census in 1899 was 28,577. The total number of schelars attending public ,i,lernentary schoels was 18,794 against 17,433, and those attending private schools 602, against 686. The electrical engineer submitted to the E'ectric Supply and Tramways Committee his quarterly report. The number of units sold during the quarter were : For lighting purposes, 39,182 ; for motors, &c., 41,71.5 ; for tramway purposes, 223,146; a total of 304,041, which was an increase of 32,947 units, as compared with the corresponding quarter of last year. A letter was read from the South Lancashire Tram ways Company asking for the Corporation's permission to make a junction with the St Helens tramway at the Elsydock end, but it was resolved that the consideration of the matter be deferred, in order that the 'lowa Clerk might make inquiries.— Mr Leach urged that they should do every- thing' to facilitate the operations of the Tramways Company, as tne connection in vestion would have the effect of bringing very many passengers into St Helens.—Mr Alderman Beecham said they were in communication with the Company, Mod the Town Clerk said be had had an interview, with Mr B Atherton, who was going to write to bim next week.—The Mayor said he did not think the tramways was ready yet, and they would do nothing to obstruct it.—The minutes were confirmed. The Director submitted to the Technical Eeucation Committee a report of the result of the examinations held last session, showing that 554 students were pre; sented, with the following result :—Distinction, 9.6 first-class, 70 ; Second class, 177; pass or third e1a58,137; failed, 174. The Director also submitted the following extract from the report issued by the Board of Education on science and art schools and classes :—" It is becom- ing increasingly evident that if any great progress in the direction of grouped courses is b be made in the future, it will be necessary for committees of the larger technical institutes to insist upon their students attend- ing definite courses of instruction. Moral suasion has been tried and found wanting. Many committees also feel the necessity of resorting to soino sort of compulsion in the best interests of the'students, although they are naturally reluctant to take a step which, however de- sirable,might tempo:arily reduce the nuMber 3f Students in attendance. It is very interesting, therefore, to record in this connection that this bold step has been taken by the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Borough of St. Helens, They decided last session that all new students should attend, unless their previous training rendered it unnecessary a compulsory prepara- tory course for one year before proceeding for more specialised Selene's and technological courses. This pre- paratory course, which necessitates attendance for three nights a week, included instruction in English, practical mathematics, geometry, and general elementary science, theoretical and practical. The success of the acneme has been remarkable. No less than 108 students entered for this course,and their attendance has been exception- ally good tnroughout, averaging in come classes nearly 90 per cent. In view of the excellent results obtained the committee have decided to extend the principle to a series of grouped courses which have been drawn up for various departments of science and technology. Other committees in the district have been watching this experiment with keen interest, and its success will probably induce souse of them to adopt a similar course where the conditioos are favourable "—Mr Martin, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the remarks of the Board of Education on their schools. They were often depreciated in St Helens, and it was satisfactory to see that, from an educational point of view, the town was called attention to as one of the foremost places in that special direction.—The minutes were confirmed. On the proroesal of the Mayor, it was decided that the illuminated address which was prepared to be sent to the King and Queen on the occasion of the Coroaation should now be sent.

Earlestown Football aub's Prospects. The usual preliminary canter of the Earlestown foot- ball club took place on the hiesnea ground on Saturday, the first team forwards being pitted against the first team defence. The attendance was decidedly encourag- ing and clearly shows that the sterling football dis- played by the eleven last season has awakened an in- terest among football enthusiasts in the district, an interest which has for year's lain dormant. The for- wards proved to be a very capable quartette as is shown by the fact that they found the ' net on five occasions, and in addition were constantly hovering round Robin. Of course the per- formances of the new captures were most anxiously watched, and winout exception they gave every satis- faction. Stanton, the new outside right from Liverpool, made a very favourable impression, showing a rare turn of speed and centring with unusual accuracy. Turton p at centre forward also gaveromle of developing into a good successor to Dawson, and although he is rather on the slow side, he keeps his wingmen well together, and what is more important he knows where the goal lies. Nothing need be said about Limoni, as his capabilities are too well known to need comment. The same remark also applies to Robin, who keeps goal finely, and will undoubtedly prove t 3 be one of the best custodians in the Lancashire League. Altogether, the play of the probable league team as a whole leaves very little room for improvement and the committee of the Club are to be complimented on hav- ing got together such & splendid combination. The season will be opened to-morrow (Saturday) when a visit will be pail to Staly bridge Rovers, the correspond- ing match last year resulting in a goalless draw. The following team will represent Earlestown goal ; Leigh and Cottam, backs ; Pennington, White- house and Limond, half-backs; Stanton, Barlow,Tiarton each and Settle, forwards.

div.head: CORONATION PROCESSION AT WARRINGTON. ---- The Mayor and the Friendly Societies.
div.p: THE CORONATION PROCESSION AT WARRINGTON. ---- The Mayor and the Friendly Societies.

We have received the following copies of correspond- ence which has takes place between the Mayor (Mr Charlton Parr) and 1r D Huighton (hon. secretary of the Frieudly Societies Council.) Town Hall.Warriegtan, August 26th 1902. _ _ _ . .

Dear Sir,—On the occasion of the last winding up meeting of our Coronation Committee yesterday, I wan glad to take the opportunity of congratulating the members on the great success which had attended their efforts, and of thanking them heartily for the assistance they had givers ma as Mayor in the promotion and execution of our Coronation Celebrations. All have worked in harmoniously and energetically that it has been • pleasure to ass and to everybody concerned, and I would ask you now that it is over to express my grate- ful aeknowledginents and heartfelt appreciation of the work done to each and all who had athand in it. The Foienely Societies' display was not oaly a credit to them- I selves but also A credit to our County Borough, and the adnairab'e order and dlsoipline maintained,logether with the picturesque effect of their devices and designs should hays made every individual citizen if Warrington as it made me. proud of the public spirit and patristic loyalty of our good old town. I hope we shall all look back with pleasurable fetlings to cur Coronation year, and while thanking God for our King's reetoration te health, with his magnificently sisecessful erownine and that of our Gracious Qtreen Alexandra, we may also,l I feel sere, rejoice in the opportunity it bait given us of recognizing that we may add to our happiness by giving happiness to others, and by extending the right hued of fellowship to all our poorer b.ethren and to those who stand in need of our kindness and support. Believe me, yours very faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR, Mayor.

Druids Hall, Seakey-atreet, August 306, 1902. D.ar Mr. Mayor,—l beg to aeknowledgo receipt of your kinJ letter, thanking all who had taken port in the Friendly Societies procession on 9th of August. I /ball bays pleasure in laying it before the next general meeting of the Council. It is pleasing to have our efforts recognised and appreciated by the Chief Magistrate of the town, and will have a tendency to encourage our members to take a greater pride and pleasure in the 51.13CP51 of our Orders. The representatives on the Town Hall COM- mittees have pleasurable recollections of all that their duties brought them in contact with, and were quite at ease in their work, particularly lav the kind and cour- teous Way you always received them. Your sympa- thetic reference at one of our meetings in the loss we had nustainod by tie dealt' of our respected Chairman, Bro. John Emson, greatly impressed Us. and will long be remembered as a noble tribute to a worthy officer.— Sincerely thanking you for your kindness, I am, dear Mr. Mayor, yours very respectfully, D. HOUGHTON, Friendly Societies Council. J. C. Parr, Eq., Mayor.

At noon to-day (August 20th), writes a Montreal correspondent, the eimple and impressive marriage service of the Church of England was performed at Christ Church Cdthedral, Moutreal, when Robert ,1 Ashton, on of the late Colonel Ashton, of Frodsh am Cheshire, England,was married to Miss Ida A Knell. Miss Knell comes directly from Paris,where she has follond her post graduate studies at the Sorbonne University of Paris The Rev H J S Boyle officiated. Later in the afternoon the young married couple left for the Thousand Islands, where they will pass come tirne before going to their home in Morris- burg,Ontario.

NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
lIINCORN Y. RUNLET.

This match was played at Runcorn on Monday afternoon. There was a moderate attendance. loth clubs played repre- sentative teams. Butterworth, in spite of his injured knee, turned out, Houghton playing at the rear of the peek. The home team lest Use toss and had to play against a strong sun' After a brief incursion into the visitors' territory dessiltory play followed in mid-Reid. Jolly, losing the ball, let Hunslet in. A. moment later Richardson get the leather away nicely, Mitchell knocking oa which left the advantage for some time with Runcorn. Rventually Ho-Hey got the ball away and following up his kiok collided violently with Houghton. Ist consequence the game was held up for some minutes. Some very pretty play followed.Lunn dribbling down finely and being stopped in the niek of time by Jones4Hanslet still , maintained the pressure and for a time Ransom were pen- ned in their own 25. Jolly averted a possible disaster by finding touch in midfield. A bit of play initiated by Rich- ardson nearly resulted in a store, the ball being lost, after heving been handled by all the home backs. Runcorn still maintained the pressure and a fine exalting burst, between Jolly, Butterworth and Warder resulted In Richardson scoring beneath the posts. Firmer easily added a goal. Runcorn still kept the visitors on the run and had hard lines a moment later in not scoring, Mitchell kicking dead when Williams was about to droo on the ball. The visitors were still kept on the defence but repeated free kicks brought re- lief. Houghton saved in grand style a dangerous rush and a moment later beat Horly by kicking dead when a score seemed imminent. Scrurnmeging on the line ensued, Hunslet keeping up the attack in fine style. Runcorn conld not withstand the pressure litd a neat piece of play was cappel by A Goldthorpe dropping a goal. The home contingent went away with a rush after this reverse, Butterworth handling the leather and after a magnificent dodgy ran moored be- tween the posts, Farmer converting. Half-time, Runcorn two goals, two tries, Hunelet a dropped goal. On resuming desultory play folloyved,Runcorn having slightly the best of matters. A fine round of lassoing was spoiled by Jones failing to take the oass at the right moment. Riehardson relieved and Houghton Caine to the fore with a neat run which planed 11 unslet on the defence. Shortly after Jones gathired anti sheered throegh his *moments, grounding the leather at the corner. Jolly failed at goal. A series of exchanges left the a-frontage with the home team, Jolly kicking a fine goal from the serum. Uninteresting play followed, Hunalet at length getting oa the home line. The danger was averted however, for a time. Just on time Whitley kicked to W Goldthorpe who passed to!.a. Goldthorpe and that rillyer scored between the posts. the goal kick failing. Final : Runcorn, three goals,three tries ; Hunelet, one goal,one try.

div.head: DIFFERENT WAYS OF BECOMING DEAF.
div.p: DIFFERENT WAYS OF BECOMING DEAF.

It is a curious fact, but none the less true, that a very large proportion or the most obstinate forms of deafness have their beginning in a simple cold in the head. Tne ffrat time such a condition occurs it usually passes away when the cold is relieved,but the hearing seldom becomes perfect again. The defect remaining, however, is generally so Blight as to escape notice, and here lies the danger, for with each successive cold the weakened organ of hearing mains further damage, until the vic- tim of this insidious farm of deafness is suddenly aroused to the fact that ene-half or one-third of the hearing power has disappeared. Besides the direct influences of a cold, another large proportion of serious Cases ef deafness find an origin through the extension of a chrinic disease of the nose or throat, by way of the eustachian tube, into the middle ear. A third cause eta very great number of oases of defective hearing is scarlet fever. An ear disease from tbis source usually produces deafness associated with a running ear, a serious matter to deal with, as a neglect- ed discharge from the ear may at any time endanger the life isf the patient. Among the less frequent causes of ear diseases may be noted blows on the ear or on the head, improper use of pint, hairpins or toothpicks to remove wax frees the ears, and various constitutional diseases, such as diphtheria, measles, rheumatism and gout. A great many illnstrations of these different harass of deafness are to be found in the last number of " The Journal for the Deaf," together with an interesting de- scription of a simple method of treating such diseases by external application, the Drouet treatment. As this, method is rapidly taking the place of the older forms of treatmeet, and is eff-cting restoration of hearing in cases hitherto prononnced incurable, its success is becoming world wide. In fact, so important is the new treatment, that the editor of the 6. Journal " has for sometime nasoed issued a " Supplement," giving the details of the cases owed each month by this method.

One very iateresting cue of deafnees of fifteen years duration can be taken from the July " Supplement" by way of illustration. This is the case ef Mr R Kirkup,of 15, Lodge-t.rracr, Hendon, Sunderlend. The ailment began in childhood, and since then the patient became very deaf. There was also greet annoyance from noises in the ears and from a peculiar feeling of dulness in the head. Catarrh of the noes and throat were severs com- plications. The entirely satisfactory result obtained from the Drouet Treatment was reported on May 17th, anti again confirmed as a complete cure on June 18th, in the following words :—" I write again reporting sayeelf cured. The discharge from my noise and threat has dis- appeared, and my hearing Is quite well. I deferred from writing for some time te see if the ouro continued, which I am glad to say it has." Those who are interested in reading a full description of tbe Drouet treatment for deafnexe and diseases of the ear, nose, and throat can obtain a free copy of the '6 Journal for the Deaf," with the" Svpplement " con- taining detailed accounts: of the cases cured during the past month by addressing the Secretavv, Drouet Ineti- tote, RozAnt's-park-ron4, Gendoo, N.W.Each Jeurnal is accompanied by a Patient's Lenart Form which en- ables applicants to receive full particulars for applying the treatment at home. div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORATION
GAS DEPARTMENT.
Annual. Report.

Mr William S Haddock (gas engineer) has just issued his fourteenth annual report of the Warring- ton Corporation Gas Department for the year end- ing March 31st, 1902. "The gas buildings and manufacturing plant:" he says, "have been kept in a good state of repair.. I am very pleased we have been so successful during the past year as the indications a year ago were unfavourable, and several of the Lancashire Gas Works have been unable to work at a profit. The large increase in the consumption of gas brought in nearly £3,000 extra and contributed largely to our success. To maintain our position it is necessary to sell gas at as low a price as possible and I hope we may soon be able to reduce our price. Our pros- pects this year are much brighter than they were 12 months ago. The price of coal is 10 to 15 per cent. lower and the value of residuals is better than they were last year. The increased make of gas is 20,442,300-5 9 per cent. upon last year's produc- tion."

In a table showing the working results it appears that the coal and cannel carbonized were 35,196 tons 2 ewts as compared with 33.645 tons 6 cwts last year. The as made was 361,502,700 cubic feet against 341,060,400 last year. The gas wade per ton was 10,262 cubic feet against 10,137,the gas sold and accounted for was 311,074,814 cubic feet against 320,501,804, and the gas unaccounted for , 22,016.886 against 21,304,596 a year ago. The aver- age illuminating power of the gas is stated to be 18.58 cani les.

The profit and loss account shows a profit on the year's working of £10,725 83 9d. Of this sum £B,OOO is required for interest on loans, &c, and the remainder goes in relief of rates. The salaries in connection with the department total up to £1,886 14s 6d, the chief officials' salaries being : Mr W S Haddock (engineer), £450; F Taylor (secretary), £250; Mr W S Howard (cashier), £230; Mr S B Chandley (assistant engineer), £170; Mr E J Smith (clerk), £150; Mr It Hind (clerk), £lO4.

div.head: Old Music Hall.
div.p: The Old Music Hall.

At the Borough -FoliCe---(5O-ur.t.O.ti- Monday the Mayor and other magistrates sat for the purpose of renewing the music licences in town. The Chief Constable said he had no objection to any of the existing licences but be wished to call the attention of the magistrates to the licence in connection with the hall in the Market-place,formerly known as the Old Music Hall, the licensee of which was the well- known and respected licensed victualler,Mr Cromp- ton, of the Blackburn Arms, It had bean suggested that as he sub-let the hall ta another gentleman— Mr Wilkinson—who actually conducted the dancing classes, it would be a more satisfactory arrangement to the bench and to him (Mr Talbot) if Mr Wilkinson held the licence. Mr Crompton felt that the hall being detached from his own house—which be conducted satisfactorily—he could not exercise that supervision over it which the Bench thought necessary. Mr Wilkinson bad not given proper notice of the application, and he (the Chief Constable) asked for an adjournment for three weeks, so that be could make the necessary in- Attiries. The Beach agreed.

Oldham Wakes i always a time when many young couples undertake the bonds of matrimony. They have been saving up their money in the wakes clubs through- out the year,aud amongst the working people it is a very common custom to seize upon the general holiday as a suitable date for entering double harness. On Monday there were some scores of marriage ceremonies per- formed in Oldham, all the parsirse of every denomina- tion being busy. All the ceremcnies lid not, however. pass off without a bitch. The Rev C N Sergeant was about to tie the fatal knot en one couple at Christ Church, Chadderton. and at that point in the service where the officiating minister has to ask whether any person can show cause or just impediment why these two persons should not be joined in holy matrimony, the mother of the bridegroom. who was present in the church, but not as are invited guest, rose and emphatically stated her objectioo to the cere- mony being completed. Her objoction was based on the fact that her son was not yet 17 years of age. As she persisted in opposing the merrier, the Vicar was com- pelled to leave the pair half married, and the pirty left the church. Outside the building the consoientious objector was the object of a hostile detionetration from a crowd of neighbours, and there was an unpleasant scans for a few minutes. Later in the day, however, the lad, was prevailed upon to withdrawn her opposi- tion, and she wrote a note to the clergyman signifying her willingness to allow the wedding to procee I. The vicar therefore fixed Tuesday afternoon for the comple- tion of the ceremony.

A correspondent writes to " Country Life " :—" A rather funny scene took place a little while age in an aviary, which shows the demoralizing effect confine- ment may have on birds of fairly good character. A starling was building its nest, and could not find any- thing to line it with in the aviary, which was certainly somewhat bare. Not to be outdone, he watched his opportunity, and caught hold of the tail feathers of a golden pheasant which wee strutting about the floor. The pheasant naturally objected, though only mildly, to this insult, and finding, after one or tufo jerks, that the otarling held on, set off at a run round the aviary. This did not shake off the attentions of the smaller bird, which ran after the pheasant like a email puppy at the end of a long ohain, and at net succeeded in strip- ping off a large piece of down, with which he departed to his nest, When he returned the pheasant was on his I guard,and seeing the starling come behind him whisked his tail from one side te the other, the starling hopping backwards and forwards in the most ridiculous manner ; when he did catch hold the pheasant tried to peck him, but, hanging firmly in, he hopped agilely oat of the way. The pheasant then put back his feet and hie shoulders forward nod pulled ; the starling put his feet forward and leanince bask pulled again, in which tug-if-war the other side of the feather was strimeed. This atnuaing robbery went on till the pheasant had but . .
three long skeleton feathers to trail after him, when the sterling, seeing nothing more was to be Rot out of him, retired into private life and the cares of a family."

New Guardian for the Warrington Union. Nominations for the post of guardian to repre- sent the East Ward of the township of Haydock on the Warrington Beard, were received on Friday. The vacancy had been caused by the non-attend- ance of MriP Canliffe,notwithstandin,g that Haydock is one of the very few townships which contribute to the travelling expenses of guardians. Only one person was nominated—viz., Mr John Turton and he was declared elected without a contest. Band of Hope Union's Novel Application. The Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union are applying to the Board of Trade for a liceece—net a drink licence, of course —but a licence directing that an association under that title shall be registered with limited liability without the addition of the word " Limited "to its name. The objects for which the association is to be established are numerous, and it requires all the letters of the alphabet,from a to v, to specify them. Amongst these may be mentioned the taking over as a going concern and to carry on the work of the temperance reform hitherto carried on by the present unincorporated union; to spread the principles and secure the practice of total abstinence from alcoholic drinks among all classes of society ; to assist in forming and sustaining a Band of Hope Union in every town and suitable district in the counties of Lanca- shire and Cheshire ; to endeavour to secure the establishment of a Band of Hope in every Sunday school: to arrange public temperance meetings and sermons ; to promote the scientific study of the properties of alcohol ; to oppose the granting Of licences or certificates and transfers for the sale of intoxicating liquors in any case where, after due coneideration of the circumstances, it may seem to the union that a house for which any such licence has been granted has been improperly conducted ; to acquire, establish, and maintain or subsidize clubs, libraries, laboratories, musical societies, &c-, to pr omote the Cause of temperance ; and to borrow or raise any moneys required by the union upon such ter ms and on such securities as may be determined. Objections to the application must be placed before the Bo ard of Trade on or before September 22nd. Underground Telegraph Wires to Warrington. At a meeting of the Council of the Hull Chamber of Commerce, on Monday, the following letter wag read :—" In reply to your letter of the 11th, I am directed by the Postmaster-General to state for the information of the Hull Chamber of Commerce that the underground telegraph system from London to the North is being extended this year as far as Warrington, where it will join the existing under- ground line between Manchester and Liverpool. Next year the Postmaster-General hopes to have sufficient funds to continue the line, not only in s northerly direction towards Scotland, but also is an easterly direction towards Leeds and Bradford. The extension, when fully carried out, will ensure practical security of telegraphic communication to the principal Yorkshire towns; but to prevent mis- apprehension I am to explain that it will take time to carry out, and that there will not be an under- ground connection with every large town. The object is to provide an alternative means of com- munication in those parts of the country which are subject to destructive storms, and to guard against the isolation of large districts. lam to add, more- over, that the underground system is not intended for long-distance telephone communication, as lorg underground lines are unsuitable for telephone working." WARRINGI ON EDUCA- TIONAL FACILITIES.
'roposed Higher Grade Elementary School.

The Museum and Techniaal Instruction Committee has issued the following report,prepared by Mr Madeley, on the subject of a proposed new day school. "In a report on the new technical school dated January 3rd, 1900, reference was made to the desirability of providing accommodation for two day departments, which it had been suggested might be included in the scheme, viz : The Pupil Teachers' Centre and a Higher Grade Mixed School. Accommodation for these departments has not been provided in the portion of the building now being erected, but arrangements have been made for the com— mittee to take over the management of the Pupil Teachers' Centre, and to distribu.e the classes amongst such rooms as are available. HIGHER GRADE ELEMENTARY SCHOOL. . The question of providing • higher grade school is not less pressing than it was two years ago,and it may now be desirable to state more definitely the kind of School which the committee have in view.

The term higher grade has now become obsolete and the type of School formerly understood by it is no longer recognized. In place of it the Board of Education has set up three grades of School, one elementary and two secondary. The first, called a higher elementary school, appears to be the type which would best meet the want which the committee proposes to supply. It will per- haps be convenient if we speak 3f it fur the moment as a higher grade elementary school. The following are characteristics which such a school would possess :

1. It would as a rule include only pupils who had previous y spent not less than two years in a public elementary school,who would be expected to enter at eleven or twelve, and in any case would not be admitted under ten years of age. 2. It would provide a definite four years' course carrying on such pupils up to the age of 15, and the, ability to profit by this course would be a further condition of admission. 3. As the school would probably be small the classes would be mixed. 4. Tne school fee to be paid by the scholars would be governed by the code of the Board of Education, according to which, as it stands at pre- sent, the amount charged could not in any case exceed ninepence a week, and if thought well, might be much less. 5. The curriculum would be based upon the pre- vious training of pupils in ordinary Elementary schools. The object in view would be the prepara- tion of the pupil for the life of a wage-earner 'in industrial or commercial occupation, and whilst purely technical instruction would be avoided, the school would naturally lead to the Technical School, for which it would provide a complete preparation.

The following subjects would probably be included, some of them being a matter of choice according as the pupils were intended for an industrial or commercial life, writing, commercial forms, shorthand, drawing (mechanical and freehand, design and modelling), English (reading and recitation, composition, grammar, literature), French, German, history, geography,life and duties of e citizen, mathematics (arithmetic, mensura- tion, algebra, geometry), science (physics, chemistry, physiography, domestic science), manual training, (woodwork, neadlework, cookery, housewifery), physi- cal exercise and singing. It seems very probable that such a school as is here indicated would supply a deficiency in the educational facilities of the town which is very widely felt. There is a class of children in the elementary schools for which those schools do not sufficiently provide, that is, those children who have passed through the seventh standard and whose parents are willing for them to continue at school for one or two years longer. The first necessity in this matter is he provision of a suitable building, and I beg to suggest that immediate steps be taken to carry out the remainder of the build- ing scheme which has already been approved by the Council. If this could be proceeded with at once it might be practicable to open the proposed higher grade school in the Autumn of 1903.

div.head: SECONDARY EDUCATION.
div.p: SECONDARY EDUCATION.

It is generally assumed throughout the country that some considerable change or development is required in regard to secondary schools. Wbat, if anything, should be done in Warrington must be a subject for careful thought, but the committee will not wish to move with- out giving full consideration to the position occupied by the Boteler Grammar School, as a richly endowed secondary school for boys. If, however, the Education Bill now before Parliament should pass, the Town Coun- cil will be placed in a position of much greater responsi bility and authority in regard to secondary education . _ .

than that which it now occupies. It may be well,there- fore, to delay further discussion of this part of the question until the final form and fate of the Bill ale known. But with regard to the first part of this report action need not be delayed. The Education Bill, if passed, will not make any change in the conditions, and the Council would be able to maintain the School by means of the Customs anti Excise Grant. CHARLES MADELEY, Secretary. 23rd July, 190 E.
