div.head: latter to tbe EVltor.
div.p: latter to tbe EVltor.
The Cycle Parade—Wonders at warrington.

Sir,—Public curiosity is indeed very great, but per- haps nowhere so great as at Warrington on the occa- sion of the cyclists' and harriers' charity carnival. Thee were inumerable objects in last Saturday's stupendous show which required more than a cursory glance to satisfy the onlookers, despite the paraders most earnest endeavours to make obvious Lis character. Wonders never cease. Those competitors who trusted solely to their ingenuity and decorative illustrativeness generally arouse the curious and bring down upon themselves all sorts of titles. For instance, and I might here explain my forte in the art of. cycle decorating is " classic original," the character which I represented and which won first: prize " most original costume" (cyclists) was a puzzle to scores, although the idea that I was representative of sport appears unanimous " What's tbis ?" echoes on all sides., and no one guesses aright. A " Pot-hunter" is evidently an unknown quantity with the " Man in the street." The thief feature of my "get-up " was easily under- stood—" grabbing the cup," said Tom, Dick,and Harry. In those few words was my whole design— the " Pot-hunter." " Pots," with the athletic competitor does not however mean cups only, but prizes. To enumerate the various strong points attached to my "wondrous wheel" is to ask too much of any kindly disposed Editor. But I cannot really close this missive without expressing my gratification veth the entire arrangements for last Saturday's brilliant parade. The behaviour of the spectators towards the procession- ists from start to finish was most exemplary. In mv humble opinion the Warrington Cycle Carnival of 1902 has few equals and only the superior, viz, Liverpool. Thanking you for courtetieS extended, yours faith- fully,
E. BATTERSBY (" Pot-Hunter,"). 29, Mauderville-street, Liverpool.

div.head: Corporation Tramways.—A Suggestion.
div.p: The Corporation Tramways.—A Suggestion.

Sir,—The suggestion I here offer is so obvious that it must have been made before, but if so its repetition is evidently necessary to ensure its being carried out. Why should there not be an additional penny stage between (say) Bank Quay Bridge and Warrington Bridge ? It seems a very unwise policy to make the charge for a short journey across the centre of the town, where the I day population is greater, just double what it is from I the centre to either extremity. I am sure my sugges- tion would be of great benefit to the public, and of con- siderable profit to the Corpsration.—YoursStc., F. E. POWELL, 8t James' Vicarage, Warrington.

div.head: ST. HELENS AND THE CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT. Stores Assistants Agitate for Higher Wages.
div.p: ST. HELENS AND THE CO-OPERA- TIVE MOVEMENT. Stores Assistants Agitate for Higher Wages.

In regard to the fight between the St Helens traders and the local Co-operative Society a meeting of the ue.cly Formed St Helens Private Traders' Employees' Association was held on Tuesday night, when the rules were adopted. The object of the Association is to support no trades- man who deals with the stores, and to assist the masters in their fight in every possible way. It was reported that the result of the combination of shop assistants was that the stores assistants, who had been excluded from membership, had applied for increased wages from the executive ot the St Helens Co-operative Society, who bad stated that if they would bring evi- dence to prove that private traders' assistants were better paid their wages would be increased. A deputation from the stores, therefore, waited on their brethren with the object of getting the necessary information, but the chairman stated that the shop assistants were cot going to help the Co-operative assistants by giving them the Information which they sought. One speaker strongly advised those members who were living with Co-operative members to leave their lodgings.

div.head: _ TRADE UNIONISTS AND THE MOVEMENT.
div.p: _ TRADE UNIONISTS AND THE MOVEMENT.

Mr J. A. Seddon tSt Helens), in proposing a vote of thanks to the whole mf the fraternal delegates at the Trade Union Congress,on Wednesday said that he:wished to make a statement in contradiction ta the rumours circulated by the press in reference to the dispute between co-operators and private traders in St. Helens that the trade unionists of the town were supporting the tatter against the former. As president of the Trades Council of St. Htlens he had to say that the trade unionists of St Helens were determined to secure fair conditions for bcth co-operators and private traders. Mr. M'Plaerson (Shop Assistants) seconded the resolu- tion, which was adopted. LEEDS PRIVATE TRADERS AND CO-OPERATIVE

div.head: STORES.
div.p: STORES.

At a meeting of the Leeds Chamber of Trade held on Wednesday night, and presided over by Mr G R Wood- cock, the circular sent out by the Sr. Helens Traders' Defence Association with regard to private traders and the competition of co-operative societies was considered. The meeting, which represented various trades and associations in the town, felt that there was much in what the St Helens organisation had placed before them. The press had hinted at a proposed boycott, but it was stated that nothing o! the kind was contemplated. It was pointed out that many Frivate traders were MM. berg of the Leeds Industrial Co-operative Society, and it was decided to draft a circular condemning such mem- bership. A further meeting is to be held with reference to the distribution of the oil cular. A PROPOSED FEDERATION OF TOWNS.

The St, Helens traders met on Wednesday night at the Fleece Hotel under the chairman3bip of Councillor J Green, the president of the Traders' Defence Associa- tion. There was a large and enthusiastic attendance. The Chairman said be had personally received letters from York, Harrington, Slingsby (Yorkshire),P/ymouth, and Chesterfield asking fcr information with a view to falling into line with St Helens. If they did so, it would strengthen their bands very considerably. He understood.the quarterly balance-sheet was due from ~be stores, and he was told that it showed an increase of membership and an increased turnover during the last quarter. The traders bad not been in harness yet for a quarter, and probably the next quarter would be the time in which they would he best able to judge what influence their defence association bad had. There could be no question they had succeeded in withdrawing a large number from the stores. It was self-evident this must be so if they carried out the principles set forth in their circular,and resolved not to support those who were purchasing at the stores. The withdrawals from the stores showed that the traders were making progress. Mr E Hebron asked if there was any definite informa- tion as to the withdrawal of the president of the Co operative Stores. Isir G Stringfellow said be had had an interview with Dlr Killey, and he assured him definitely that he had severed all connection with the Co-operative Society. Mr W H Perkins said the time had come when they should see what could be done in carrying the advocacy of their movement direct into some cf the adjacent towns. The committee might arrange deputations, and directly they got a few towns in Lancashire organised they could federate, and then they would he able to deal with the manufacturers. At present the co-opera- tive stores were taking a mean advantage of many of the manufacturers. Next week the com- mittee work would begin. The traders were all in full sympathy, and they must do what they could to move the public, with whom, after all, the issue must ult'- mat.ly rest. They had got to show that the advantsees of which they spoke, and which they claimed belonged essentially to their movement, were advantages of which they cruid have the clearest evidence. In his judgment. the f-ture was bright with promise, and he felt firmly convinced that if they Rtncil together they would find the movement spreading and taking root in all parts of the country. One rf the sneakers reported that owing to Welsh coal crmiog to a Co-operative Society in the neighbour- hood of Wigan a large colliery firm in the district had , derided to 1imtgc eo•rperative members in their emp'oy, and to refuse to allow any of their houses to be tenanted by re-,•perarors. The speeches of nthrr rnrmters were of a highly op- the comnlete success of the timistin (Mara( ter rrgr rdine movement. agit waa boycnd all doubt now that it was spreading throughout the country.

IWarrinuton P.S.A. Society. The usual meet,ng of this Society W/19 bPld in the Co-operative Hall. Fankey-street, on Sunday. there beim-, an excellent attendance Mr Stott occupied the chair. Mies Armstrong delighted the audience with her rendering of" Glory to Thee my God. this night." and " The captive's prayer " Mr Irish, of Patricroft, was the sreaker, and based bis remarks on the "Life of Daniel."

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT
COUNCIL,
-- Lord Newton and the Common.

The monthly meeting of this Coun:il was held at the Town Ball, Earlestown, on Monday evening, Mr T Demand presiding. There were also present :—Messrs CB F Borron, A t Smith, W Gilmour, J Simpson, W E T Evans, F J Wood, Dr Latham, Dr Patterson, with C Cole (,clerk), R T Surtres (fliompon N Siddeley, water engineer), and A Bowes (surveyor). _am

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

- At a meeting of this c3mmittee a further letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to'the sanction issued by that Board on the 21st. January, 1334, authorising the borrowing by the Newton-in- Makerfield Improvement Commissioners of the sum of £5,000 for purposes of a Cemetery,and pointing out that as the Function was given in respect of the items speci- fied in the estimate forwarded to that Board cn the 9h November, 1883, it should be returned to that Board for cancellation t 3 the extent to which it had not been acted upon. The Local Government Board also wrote with respect to the information required by them when con- sidering an applicatioa for sanction to a loan for the pur- pose of purchasing land for extending the Cemetery. It was resolved that the sanction referred to in the letter from the Local Government Board be returned to the Board for cancellation in the manner pointed out by them.
The minutes were approved on the proposition ot Dr Patterson incmded by Mr Simpson. TECEINICAL INSTRUCTION.COMMITTEE._

_ A circular letter was read from the Director of Edu- cation of the County of Lancaster, at a meeting of this committee, stating that the County Technical Instruc tion Committee was prepared to recommend a grant o £162 to the Council ire aid of technical instruction fo the year 1902-3, and enclosing form of agreement. It was resolved that the offer of the County Technical Instruction Committee be accepted,and that the Council be recommended to order its common seal to be affixed to the'sgreemenr. In answer to Dr Latham the Chairman said the matter would come before the committee again before the grant was transferred to the Viaduct Technical Instruction Ccm nittee. THE QUALITY OF EAELESTOWN GAS.

COMPLAINF FROM Ti3E CO-OPERATINE SOCIETY. The minutes of the Gas Committee contained a report by Mr Francis Jones. M.Sc., F.R.S.E.. Manchester,upon the condition of the gas works at Esrlestown and the illuminating power and composition of the gas. Mr Jones stated that he found the arrangements of the works in every way suitable for the manufacture of gas. The gas was teeted for illuminating power and was tound equal to 19-06 standard candles. Mr Jones gave the result of his analysis of samples of the gas. At a meeting of the committee it was resolved that further analyses of gas be made, and that the matter be left to the chairman of the committee. A letter was read from the Secretary of the Earlestown Industrial Cc-operative Society, complaining of the poor quality of the gas supplied thoughout the township. It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to inform the Co- operative Society that the matter Is receiving the attention of this committee. It was resolved that the Engineer be directed to proceed with the laying of the gas main for the supply of gas to the Sankey Sugar, Works,and other property in connection with the works The following report of the staff committee was read and adopted, viz :—The clerk read to the committee the application received frnm the leading stokers at the gas works for a week's holiday with full pay, and submitted oarticu!ars as to the hnlid sys granted at other gas works in the neighbourhood. Resolved : That the clerk in- form the atokers that the committee does not see its way to grant their request."

div.head: ihe miautes Were confirmed. WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: ihe miautes Were confirmed. WATER COMMITTEE.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the application of the Council for sanction to borrow £B2l, to defray the cost of provid- ing new mains,services, and meters during the next five years, and stating that as it was contrary to their practice to sanction a loan to cover prospective expendi- ture over a period of more than three years, they must limit the sanction (which was enclosed and dated the 14th instant) to a loan of £493 (i.e., three-fifths ot £821) to cover three years' expenditure. The Local Govern- ment Board alio stated that they were prepared to con- sider furtber the application as regards the sum of £1,779 paid out of revenue from the Ist April, 1897, to the the 30th September, 1901, and requested to be supplied with full information ai to the circumstances in which the borehole was sunk, and as to the results obtained, together with a detailed statement of the ex- penditure of the sum of £1,779, and plans showing the situation of the works carried out. As regards the amended application made for sanction to borrow £18,900 for the purposes of the water undertaking, the Board stated that they would direct a further local 1 ' inquiry to be held as soon as the other engagements of their Inspectors would permit. The minutes were approved.

THE COUNCIL AND HIGH-STREET, NEWTON. The Highways and Sanitary Committee again con- sidered tee question of the weeding of land in High- street, Newton-le-Willows (referred back to this committee by the Council for reconsideration) when it was resolved that the resolution passed at the meeting held on the 21st July be adhered to. It was resolved that the following report of the Destructor committee of the 14th inst be received and adopted, viz. :—" The Clerk reported with respect to his corres- pondence with Messrs P and J Bevan as to the acquire- ment of land at vitriol-Nuare for the purpose ef the erection of a house refuse destructor, and stated that Messrs Kevan were prepared to consider an offer from this Council. Resolved that a valuer be engaged to value the land, and that the valuation, when received, be referred to the Chairman, with power to instruct the Clerk to submit an offer to Messrs Kevan." It was re- solved that the following report of the Isolation Hospital Sub-Committee of the 14th inst,be received and adopted viz. :—•• The Clerk reported that on the 15th May, 1897, Mr Pardey, the then agent to the late Lord Newton, wrote to the Clerk to the Council as fellows: • I have great pleasure in informing you that Lord Newton is prepared to meet the wishes of your Council by provid- ing land upon which to erect an 'lsolation Hospital ' The question of site will have to be considered." The Clerk also reported that he had been informed that Lord Newton could not deal with any applications for land until the question of the ownership of the Common had been settted. The committee considered several sites which would be suitable for the erection of the Hospital. Resolved that thb Clerk be directed to write Mr Leslie (agent to Lord Newton) and ask him to kindly give the matter his consideration at the earliest possible oppor- tunity, and point out to him that for some time past the Medical Officer of Health has been urging the Council to take steps to at once erect a hospital, as the want of accommodation for the isolation of persons sufferiog from infectious diseases is a source of great danger to the t ealth of the inhabitants of this district,"

Dr Latham asked what the Fire Brigade sub-com- mittee had done with regard to the hosepipes. It would be three weeks before they met again in committee and as there was not s respectable piece of hosepipe to send to any fire in the meantime, the matter W&FI one of urgency and he thought they ought to know whether the sub-committee was proceeding rapidly in the matter. The Chairman said he could give Dr Latham his own personal assurance that the sub-committoe was pro- ceeding as gulch ly and expeditiously as possible in the matter. No time was being lost.

At the request of Mr Smith the Clerk read the follow- ing extract from the minutes of the committee submitted it the last Council meeting, which was referred to in the minute respecting the weeding of High-street :—A letter was read from Mr J Randall, complaining of the state of the footpath (between the paving and his premieel) in High-street, Newton. It was resolved "that Mr Randall be informed that the Council are quite willing to undertake the weeding of this part of the footpath, providing the owners of the land and premises abutting upon the street will give a written undertaking that the land is dedicated to the public." blr Smith moved that the matter be referred back to the committee. Ho did so because be considered that the form the resolution was absolutely hostile to the interests of the Council. There never bad been, and certainly so far as he could understand it, there never could be any question raised as to what WAS the condi- tion of the whole of High-street, Newton, and it seemed to him that it would be in the last degree against the interests of the township if for one moment they ad- mitted the slightest doubt as to the condi- tion of that street. Those members who lived there considered the street to be on of thefinest streets in any place within reasonable reach, at all events,of Newton, and for one moment to admit even the possibility of a shadow of a doubt as to whether the whole of that street was dedicated to the public would be against the Council's interests and would be strengthening the hinds of those who might possibly at some later date raise the ,1 question as to whether they had the right to set their I property forward. Mr Borron seconded.

Dr Latham said he Was very glad that Mr Smith bad I raised the question because the same opinions that he , had expressed that day were also expressed in corn• mittee. He felt certain that there ought not to be the slightest doubt as to who the land telonged to and it would be a deplorable thing to allow anyone to obtain the power of railing cf! a portion of the highway. Mr Simpson said that as a property owner in the street he claimed certain frontages belonging to his premises. Be did not give his right sway to that Council or to anyone else. He objected to the amend- ment. Mr Thompson said the matter was fully discussed at the committee meeting and they thought that in the beit interests of the Council the best course to take would be to pass the resolution. Be was sorry to go contrary to the interests of the Council and as some members were not present at the committse meeting he was willing to:support the amendment

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY. SEPTEMBER 5, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY. SEPTEMBER 5, 1902

The Chairman said there were only eight members out of fifteen present when this very vital question was decided. He thought they ought to have • greater majority present when such a resolution was passed. The amendment was put to the meeting and carried, Mr Simpson being the only member to vote against it. Dr Latham : He is looking after his own property,you see, Mr Chairman. A member : well he ought to do The other minutes were confirmed. LORD NEWTON AND THE COMMON.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee the Clerk reported with respect to the proposed application of the Provincial Electric Supply and Traction Co to the Beard of Trade for a provisional order authorising them to supply electricity for auy public or private purposes within the district. It was resolved that the whole question be referred to Council- lor A Smith and the Clerk, with instructions to report thereon to the next meeting of the committee. A letter was read from Messrs Peace and bilis stating that they had induced Lord Newton's solicitors to extend the time to the 20th inst for the Council to come to some decision as to his Lordship's offer to give up ten acres of land at the Common, on certain conditions, for the purpose of a recreation ground. It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to inform Messrs Peace and Ellis that the matter has been fully considered by this committee,who have decided tm recom mend the Council to accept Lord Newton's offer on the terms mentioned in Messrs Houseman's letter of the 16th April last, subject to the modifications as to the area and fencing of the land since agreed to, provided access is given to the land from Common-road and Earle-street.—lt was resolved that the Town Nall sub-committee be asked to report as to tbe proposed extension of the Hall. Mr Gilmour objected to the resolution as to Lord Newton's offer, because he did not know what the terms were. Was Lord Newtoa going to give them a title deed ? It was a vital question to the interests of Council and the public ought to know something more about it.
--.-. The Chairman pointed out that Mr Gilmour voted for the resolution.

Mr Gilmour : I did on certain conditions, but I don't know what the conditions are yet. (Laughter.) Mr Borron said Mr Gilmour was a member of the sub-committee which went carefully into the matter and he (Mr Barron) was depending upon him to make 8)1110 explanations as to the decision arrived at. Dr Latham asked if it was the intention' of the Coun- cil to allow the publication of the whole of the corre- spondence from beginning to end, the work that had been done with the Commons Preservation Society, and the evidence which had been collected. Ha thought, like Mr Gilmour, that the publio were not satisfied that everything had been done that ought to be doae. Per- sonally, be thought the Council were wise, to some ex- tent, in accepting Lord Newton's offer. Of course it was an offer which no one who knew anything at all about the Common could entirely accept with pleasure but it was an offer which they accepted, ho took it, as getting them out of a difficult position. He thought the public were perfectly entitled to know the whole ot the circumstances.
The Chairman said tbe question of publication was one which the committee should decide.

Mr Gilmour said the reascn the offer was accepted was because if they had gone into court they had not a particle of evidence to back up their claim. The Chairman : You had better net say any more. . _ .
Mr Gilmour contended that the public ought to know all the circumstances or else the Council would be in a dilemma. _ . . . . . . . . .

Mr Smith was of the opinion that it would not be desir- able in the interests of the Council that the correspond ence on any matter, and especially in a matter of complication such as this had been, should be laid before thiTipublie. He ventured to think that those whom they represented had confidence in them that they would look after their interest and he ventured to think they would come to the conclusion that in the resolution which had been passed the Council had been studying the best interests of the township. He thought they might safely assure their constituents that it was not before they were perfectly satisfied that there was noth- ing to justifythe Council in laying claim to the Common that they adopted the course emhodied in the resolution. The Council had done everything they possibly could do to unfathorn, if it were possible to unfathom evidence as regarded the rights which certain of their constituents claimed, and they sorrowfully came to the conclusion that there was no evidence to support these claims. He thought that when they had been bound to admit that, they must accept with pleasure the offer—it was a generous offer he considered—which Lord Newton had voluntarily made of ten acres of the Common. Dr Latham said he should move in committee that the correspondence los placed before the public. The minutes were confirmed, Mr Gilmour being the only disentient. THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT,

Dr Latham said they were glad to see the Chagrman of the Finance Committee back again. Through his ab- sence they had missed one of the most important state- ments to the Council—the annual financial statement. He hoped at the next monthly meeting the Council vronla be privileged to hear that statement. The Chairman said it was a matter for the committee to consider whether it was desirable to have the state- ment at such a late hour. The Council then rose.

div.head: ..-..-.0-. CHILDREN NEGLECTED AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ..-..-.0-. CHILDREN NEGLECTED AT EARLESTOWN.
Mother Sent to Prison.
Ann Taylor, 8, Gibraltar Cottages, Earlestown, appeared at tbe Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday to answer to the charge of neglecting her six children.

Mr Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., said this was a very bad ease. The woman had been under the supervision of Inspector Hackett since February 23rd, and had been warned time attor time about the neglect; of the children. No improvement had been made. Prisoner's husband was serving five years' penal servitude, and she was living with another man named Morris.

James Jackson, Gibraltar Cottages. Earlestown,stated that he had known prisoner about 18 months. He had given her children many a score of meals. Prisoner got drunk at times and neglected her family. The children were dirty and had no clogs nor stockings to put on. Inspector Hackett, R.S.P.C.C., said he had visited the prisoner's house many times and had advised her to go into the workhouse as she complained that she was not getting sufficient money with which to keep her children. He, however, ascertained that at least £2 a week was coming into the house. The children had scarcely any clothing.On July 11th he found a daughter, aged 11,in charge of the house. The baby was tied in a chair, and its body was black with longstanding dirt. None of the children had any shoes and stockings on their feet. Their legs were black. One of the children had sore eyes, through not washing them, and another was filthy and verminous, and had a sore nose. There was only one decent bed in the house, and the only covering was a sheet and quilt. There was no food in the house, and he never saw a more neglected family in all his experience. P.C. Clarke said that on one occasion he found the children in a pitiable condition, huddled together by the fire trying to get warm. Prisoner stated that the Inspector stopped her working seven weeks ago, and not a penny had been coming in the house since. One of her sons had been unable to work owing to illness.
iThe Chairman said the ease was a very bad one, and prisoner would have to go to gaol for two month..

div.head: EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVES AT WALTON HALL.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVES AT WALTON HALL.

The members of the Earlestown Conservative Club, with their wives and lady friends, held their annual picnic on Saturday, and an enjoyable day waa spent at Walton Hall. The picnickers assembled in the club at Earle-street at one o'clock and there took their seats in vehicles provided by the co:nmittec. The number who made the )ourney was estimated at 250. The first waggonette was occupied by the Earlestown Viaduct Band, which played inspiriting music en route to Walton Hall, the seat of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., where the day was spent. In another waggonette were the mem- bers of the committee, with Messrs W A Mawdsley and T Haselden (secretary). The journey was made by way of Newton. Winwick, Warrington, and Lower Walton, to the Hall whera the party alighted. The grounds of the Hall bad been thrown open to the visitors, who were charmed with the beautiful condition of the large fir and other trees. Thr spacious and admirably-kept greenhouses provided a never-ending source of plea- sure to the visitors, whilst the kitchen gardens were also admired. The piggeries, whidi form an attraction in themselves, were also visited, whilst many found much to interest them in the stables and well-appointed riding school. Shortly before tea time the Viaduct Band played a selection of music in front of the Hall, and when Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall appeared loud and prolonged cheers were raised. After the cheering had subsided, Sir Gilbert Greenall said that on behalf of himself and Lady Greenall he desired to exoress his pleasure in see- ing the members of the Earlestown Conservative Club at Walton. He must congratulate them on having had such a very fine day, and especially at having such a large turn-out. (Cheers). . I
At the request Of Mr 1,5.7 A Mawdsley, hearty cheers were raiged for Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenell for their kindness in allowing the party to visit the Park and Hall.

—Si; Gilbert Greensll replied, stating that be thanked 1 them very much for their appreciation of the slight ser- vice he had rendered. 1 Tea was partaken of at the Stag Hotel. Walton, and shortly after a quarter past seven the return journey was commenc.ed,Earlestown being reached in good time. The arrangements for the picnic were made by the com- mittee of the club, with Mr Haseldea as secretary. LADIES' MARKET BA.SKSTS—Wru.tiat BEswietc, 21, Buttermarket-street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.p: WARRINGTON.

Accident at the Central Station. On Monday evening Thomas Beckett, a shunter in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Railway Com- pany, who resides at Tinsley's-terrace, Warrington was conducting some shunting operations in the siding of the Central Station, and failed to notice the approach of a light engine, which knocked him down and passed over his body. He was appar- ently unaware that he was standing in the four- , foot way. He was removed to the Infirmary,where it was ascertained that be had sustained a broken leg, three broken ribs, and some wounds on the knee and head. H NI. About 50 workmen in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company were engaged on Sunday in making the alterations on the down line at Wilderspool Crossing in connection with the Corporation tramway service to Stockton Heath. Operations were commenced at four o'clock in the morning and were finished at 830 in the evening, the men being in charge of Mr Turnbull, assistant to Mr Andrews, of the Permanent Way Department. For the second time this summer the Mayor (Mr J C Parr) kindly threw open the grounds at Grappenhall Hayes to the public on Saturday. The weather was beautifully fine, and many residents in Warrington and district visited the grounds. The flowers in the conservatories and gardens were in full bloom, and were themselves a proof of the can and attention bestowed upon them by the head gardener and his staff. The Warrington Royal Cycling Club, whose original fixture was a paper chase, turned up in strong force, and,stacking their bicycles against one of the fences, made an enjoy- able tour of inspection. They, with the ocher visitors, were cordially welcomed by the Mayor and Mayoress.

div.head: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON.
NEWTON CIILTECHWORKERS' PICNIC.

On Eaturday the voluntary church workers of St Peters' Church,Newton had their annual outing,ths occasion being favoured with beautiful weather. The party'numbering 44, including the choir, bell- ringers,sidesmen &c..was in charge of Mr H Lane, and Mr Lyons, secretaries. They left Newton about nine o'clock for Blackuool,where they arrived about eleven o'clock, After a short walk along the promenade, they returned to the Royal Hotel for dinner which was excellently served and thoroughly enjoyed. The afternoon was spent in a visit to the Tower and tea was partaken of at the Royal Hotel. After tea several of the party visited the Winter Gardens whilst others spent their time on the sea front. At tea Mr Ritchie, in the absence of the Vicar who was indisposed, proposed a vote of thanks to the church workers for their services during the year, to which Mr Lane responded. The latter proposed a vote of thanks to the choir, Mr Leyland, organist, responding. A very enjoyable day was spent and the party reached home about half-past eleven.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES TOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES TOWN.
LBY A CORRESPONDENT].

The football season opened very auspiciously in Earlestown on Saturday, the premier club playing a trial match. The team has undergone a complete change since last season, there being several new players. A fairly good crowd turned up to witness the game, and this in itself is a good augury of the support the club will receive if good sport is pro- vided. Last season the gates were of a substantial character, and the club bee been enabled to clear off the few small debts which had been hanging over, and to commence the season with a Usti,- factory balance in the treasurer's hands. - The expense of running is team in the Lancashire League is very heavy, and it is hoped the football public will extend to the local club that support which is necessary to enable them to obtain and keep the best material.

Lord Newton and his agent appear to be holding a rod over the heads of the District Council. lu 1697 the late Lord Newton offered to provide a site for the erection of an Isolation Hospital. Of course the Council accepted the offer, which was considered to be a kind of Jubilee gilt, but until now they have taken no steps in the direction of erecting the hoppital. They now appear to be moving in the matter, but the present Lord Newton says he will not deal with the question until that of the ownership of the Common is settled, This is a poor way ot dealing with it. Lord Newton knows very well that the Common belongs to the people, but in effect he says," if you will say that the Common is mine, I will give you apiece of it for an Isolation Hospital. "I hope the Council will not be persuaded to barter away the rights of the people in this way. I have no doubt a section of the Council would be quite agreeable to truckle to Lord Newton, but trio others should certainly hold fast and let Lord Newton prove his right to the lane before entering into any bargain with him.

Some discussion appears to have taken place at the Council meeting as to the publication of the correspondence which ha i passed upon the Com- mon question. Mr smith said be would not be a party to giving away the rights of the public, but he did not think it would be to the best interests of the Council to publish the cJrrevondence. Why ? In what way would the interests of the Council suffer? It is a public question, and if there is any difficulty the public should be taken into the con- fidence of the Council and they might probably get 6101,0 valuable suggestions. Re made a point of the fact that Lord Newton bad offered 10 acres of the Common to the Council for a recreation ground. but of what value is it to the district? He says we ought to have accepted the offer with pleasure. Per- haps so. That 18 Mr Smith's opinion, but it is by no means the opinion of his constituents, and be- fore making a statement of that kind in public he ought to have satisfied himself that. he was express- ing the opinion of the people he represents. Dr Latham should insist upon his motion,as he has ';ne public behind him.

div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS, RuglT-FT;tball.

Football once again ! To-day the football season may be said to open in real earnest and cricketers must hie themselves to their pavilions until the foot- ballers have had their innings. The Warrington Club journeys to Swinton where "the Lions "will be found waiting patiently for their prey. Whether the " Wire- pullers '' will prove too tough remains to be seen. It is very dangerous to predict before either side has had an opportunity of showing their strength. There is already a good deal of optimism amongst enthusiasts on both sides. Swinton certainly had the advantaze last season when they won both engagements but there are good grounds for believing that Warrington will do better this year. Let us hope so.

" No greater attraction could have been secured than the Warrington team, "says a Swinton correspondent, "the Wirepullers always proving a greaVdraw.' The games between the teams are as a rule of a very close nature, one peculiarity of the results for a great number of years being that each club always managed to win on its own ground, and Swintonians will remember the traditions respecting the Warrington ground which now happily have been scattered. The teams met twice last season, Swinton winning both games, and the corresponding match on the Swinton ground ending in a victory for the 'Blues' by eight points to six."

The Swintonians evidently look upoli the scattering of last year's traditions as a " happy " consummation. It was anything but" happy" to the true Warring- tonian, and it would be some compensation to be able to return from Swinton to-day looking " happy " with two points safely netted.

Great improvements have been effected on the Swin- ton ground. The old uncovered stand has been taken down, and the ground banked up. The inner railings on that side of the ground have been advanced four yards, and thus the playing pitch has been taken more towards the new stand. This stand, which was erected after the fire last year, is now complete, an will add materially to the accommodation of the ground. A portion has been reserved for guinea ticket holders. Additional fencing has been erected, and a small stand placed near a new sixpenny entrance on the New Cross- street side. The whitewash brush had been used to advantage, new goal posts have been bought, and the turf is in splendid condition. The Warrington Committee have selected the follow- ing team for the match :—Ratcliffe, full back ; Fish, Hockenhall, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarters ; Allen and Burgess, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Forster, Edmondson, Roberts, J. Jolley, W. Swift, and J. Taylor forwards.

Tho composition of the back division will, no doubt, come as a surprise, for Hallam bad been looked to as this season's full back. He has not yet signed on, and as the committee have been unable to come to terms, we shall miss him in his accustomed place. In Rat- cliffe, Warrington have a promising understudy and, one who has shown great resource and skill on ,several occasions when he has been called upon to fill Hallam's place. His play at Swinton to-day will be watched with keen interest. Isherwood, it will be noticed, is an absentee from the three-quarter line, but it is hoped that lie will be ready to take the field in a few weeks time. Hockenhall should prove a reliable substitute. He has a good turn of speed, is dodgy and resourceful, and if he feeds Fish as unselfishly as Isherwood did, he will prove of immense value to the club and justify his selection.

The team, taken as a whole, might readily pass for one of last year's. All the players have donned the primrose and blue jersey before. Followers of the club will doubtless regret that the Committee have not secured recruits for the forward line. As it is composed to•day it is a good one, but will anyone venture to say that it will stand the strain of a whole season's work ? Unless the Club profits by last year's mistakes we shall have to lament them again at the close of the season.

By the return of Fell to South Africa, the Club has lost a finely-built forward, a loss which will not easily be filled. J. Swift is still under suspension for a little affair at the close of last season, and therefore not ava 1- able for to-day's match.

Practices were held on Saturday and Tuesday and there was a strong turnout. All the players are now in good form. The three-quarter line is an especially fast one, and given good opportunities by the forwards, they should make the Warrington scoring average a heavy one.

The Swinton team will be as follows :—D Traynor, full back ; J II Cooper, R Valentine (captain) ; W Wall- work, and H Barnett, three-quarters ; T Samuels and F A Morgan, half-backs ; 3 Evans, E Yates, R Tickle, J Preston, T Pomfret, W Cheetham, G R Jones, and R Berry, forwards. Reserve, 3 Blackburn.

Chorley, last year's full back, is unwell, having met with art accident whilst racing, Traynor is declared to be " well and fit "and is to be given a trial at full back. Hampson, as was expected, is not selected.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

There is no mistaking the fact that this season the Warrington eleven has become a combination to be reckoned with, but nevertheless, the strongest suppor- ters of the team would probably never have anticipated such a spendid victory over Leyland—one of the most powerful elevens in the county —as that which the Warringtonians achieved on Saturday- It was, indeed, a noticeable encounter, and the heartiest congratulations are due to the Warringtonians on the gratifying result of their exertions. It was only the previous Saturday that Warrington visited Leyland, and it was then ad- mitted that they accomplished a highly creditable per- formance in making a daw Saturday's engagement at Arpley, however, ended in a complete triumph for the home team. Batting first the Warringtonians had compiled the substantial aggregate of 153 when the last wicket fell. Leyland had noarly two hours in which to save the match, but the Warrington bowling land fielding was so effective, that three minutes from time the eleven had been dismissed for 83. It was an exciting finish, and, as may readily be imagined, the interest of the spectators ran very high. On returning to the pavilion the victors were warmly cheered.

Both teams were strongly represented, Mr. Stanning, who had been assisting Lancashire in their encounter with the Australians, journeyinr from Aigburth to take part in the match. There was a capital assembly of spectators.

The brilliant batting of E. A. Connor was a striking feature of the Warrington innings. By hitting freely all round the wicket, he knocked up 41 before he was caught by the Leyland captain at mid-off. His chief strokes included six fours and three threes.

W H Podmore also rendered good service, his total of 36 being compiled without a faulty stroke His innings was characterised by accurate placing all round the wicket. J Lynes, the popular professional, was in good form, and scored an acceptable 28. J W Bibby, the captain, was responsible for 11.

Too much praise cannot be bestowed upon Lynes, for his splendid bowling, and to him, in a great measure, the victory was due. The capture of six wickets for 25 runs was his gratifying accomplishment. The Ley- land batsmen were unable to make much headway, as is evidenced by the fact that J Stanning (16) and B Sharp (11) were the only players to attain double figures.

Instead of improving upon Una previous'week's form. the Second Eleven failed even to maintain it, and had to submit to defeat at Leyland, The home team went to the wickets first, and put together 122, P. Turners (27), A. Calderbank 22,,( J. Baxendale (22) and A. Jackson (14) being the most successful batsmen In response Warrington compiled only 88, E Pierpoint land Houghton being responsible for 29 and 18 respec• tively. Bennett bowled well for Warrington, taking five wickets for 37 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills entertained Moore and Daresbury and came out victorious by 38 runs. (Clarke was in good form with the willow, and knocked up 25 not out. For the visitors Woods (16) was the top scorer. Taylor bowled very effectively for the Wire Mills, taking eight wickets for 15 runs.

Crosfield's easily disposed of Litherland, knocking up 118 for the loss of only 8 wickets against their oppon- ents 39. T Whitfield (44) and W Warren (381 were the most useful batsmen, and, as regarded the bowling, G Podmore took seven wickets for 20 and B Ford three for 17,

Peter Walker and Son, Limited, had Cheshire Lines Engineers for their opponents, and gained a creditable victory by 42 runs. For the Brewery T Wright (27 not out), W Ashton .(17) and J Cain 1.71 bowled in first rate style, as did P Lawless (26) for the Engineers. E Allen worked great havoc with the ball, capturing four wickets for 9 runs.
Cycling.
C. Berry, of Warrington, carried off the first prize in the one mile handicap at Mottram sports on Saturday.

Favoured by beautiful weather " President's Day" in connection with the Lovely-Lane Cycling Club passed off with complete success on Saturday. Pick- mere was the venue selected, and thither the party journeyed on their machines, under the leadership of the Captain (Mr Rose). An excellent tea was provided and thoroughly enjoyed. Afterwards the cyclists made their way to the lake, where a boat was engaged and a
pleasant row was indulged in for about an hour. The homTward journey was then commenced and Warring- ton was reached about nine o'clock after one of the most enjoyable runs of the season.

Swimming. On Tuesday evening the outstanding attraction at the twenty-fifth annual sports of the Leander Swim ming Club, held at Woodcock-street Baths, Birmingham, was the quarter-mile race for the championship of the Mid- land Counties. The world's champions J A Jarvis, and five others started. From the outset the issue was never in doubt. Jarvis taking the lead at once, and winning by forty yards, E Gilbert, of Walsall, was I second, and H Milner, Walsall, third. 7me, smin. 56secs.
THE OHEMISTRY OF THE LEATHER TRADE.

div.head: Speech by Mr. C. E. Parker.
div.p: Speech by Mr. C. E. Parker.

Leather trade chemists from various European coun- tries,c-nnbined together in an International Avsociation, are holding their annual Conference this weak in Leeds. Thirty years ago tanners' chemists were unknown, and 15 years ago the number could be counted on the fingers. But the deve:opment of the leather trade has made new processes of tanning necessary, until the application of chemicals to the raw hide has become an exact science. The Conference, which assembled at ' the Queen's Hotel, Leeds, on Tuesday, was not a large ' one,but it was fully representative of the ;leather trade I is its varied.aspecte.

The President is a well-known tanner in the Warring- ton district, Mr Charles E. Parker. Among others attending the Conference are Herr Franz Kathreiner, Germany, an ex-President of the Association; Mr V. Boegh, Copenhagen ; Drs. Dreher, Paessler and Koerner, Freiburg, Saxony; Mr C. A. Andrers and Dr Baldracco, Turin • Dr Klock, Hamburg; Mr A. J. Borghstein, Holland ; Professor Ahnert, Dresden ; Dr A. Ganseer, Milan; Mons. Jossier, of Paris, President of the Syndi- cate of Leather Manufactarers of France; Mr R. Mellor and Mr W E Walker. President and Vice-President of the Manchester, Liverpool and District Federation of Tanners; Professor H. R. Proctor, Leeds, and Mr A. Seymour Jones, of Wrexham, ex-Presidents of the Association ; and Dr J Gordon Parker, London, the bon general tresaurer. . .

When the delegntes assembled on Tuesday morning they were heartily welcomed by the President, who was particularly gratified at the presence of the English leather trade reoresentatives. Mr R. Mellor, president of the Liverpool and Manchester Tanners' Federation, briefly acknowledged the greeting. It was announced that the Italian members had invited the Association to meet at Turin In 1904. TITE PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS. -

r In the course of his address, which was translated into German, the President expressed a hope that as the result of the gathering there might spring up a spirit of personal good feeling and common interest between the members, who, although divided by distance, national- ity, and speech, bad in trust the prosperity of leather manufacture in those phases which were controlled and I influenced by chemical action. The day had gone by,he said, when it was necessary to plead for a recognition of the value:of chemical knowledge and research in connec- tion with the leather trade. However much they might depend upon their practical experience, manufacturers I had ben forced to acknowledge that it alone was utterly inadequate to enable them to keep pace with the times. The tanner who hoped for success now-a-days could not be independent of chemical knowledge, and the tanner who relied snost on chemical aid,and wisely used it,would —other things being equal—be the most suceessful.Years ago,before chemists devoted themselve as specialists tot he industry, a good deal of harm was done and prejudice engendered among practical men by the applicaLion of the ill-digested theories of chemists who took up tanning as sort of hi-product of their time and thought. This 1 prejudice was happily dying out, thanks in a great measure to the influence of the International Association and its researches. Pleading for more research work the President said there was a goodly number of chemists connected with the various tanning schools, who were able and ready to undertake such work, but the financial help to remunerate them was wanting. Would it not, then, he asked, be a commercially sound investment for the members of the leather trade, either individually or collectively, to allocate a substantial sum for definite research work ? Delving into technical matters, Mr Parker asked whether the bide powder pro- cess was the most satisfactory that could be adopted ? He had good reason to believe, he said that two samples of the same tanning material, showing equal strength by the hide powder process, might in actual practice give very different results in weight ot leather. If this was se, he contended that they ought to be on the out- look for some better method, or some adaptation of the present method, that would give results more in har- mony with actual practice. BOOKBINDING AND SULPHURIC ACID. After transacting some general business the Confer- ence settled down to the consideration of an extensive list of technical subjects. Only one of them yielded anything of public interest. That was a conversation regarding the use of free sulphuric acid in leather. The Chairman, looking sOmtiwhat Surprised, wondered what they did with sulphuric acid in their leather at all. He did not know, he said, whether this chemical was use 3 in the Leeds tanneries, but it was certainly not used in the Liverpool and Manchester districts.

Dr. J. 431. ordcn Parker explained that some time ago Profegsor Proctor, himself, and others acted as a com- mittee to investigate the cause of the decay of leather used for book-binding. It was represented to them that the British Museum authorities bad to spend several thousand pounds every year in the renovation of books whose bindings were rotting away. .It was found that nine-tenths of this decay arose from the use of sulphuric acid as a bleaching agent, and as used to bring up the strong colour of the dye-stuff. As much as 3 to 5 per cent. of free sulphuric acid had been found in some leathers, which, it was needless to say, went to pieces in the course of three or four years. An instance had come under the attention of a London Library where the bookbindings were found to contain PEI per cHst of sulphuric acid, This library was recommended to adopt pigskin as being the most durable for binding, but now, after six years' wear, the bindings could be ripped with the finger nails. When sulphuric acid had once come in contact with leather no washing, however strong, would totally remove it,

•-- In the afternom th 3 delegatss were entertained rn luncheon at the Queen's Hate! by the British section of the Association. Mr C E Parker p-esided. Subs,quently the members of the Conference paid a visit to tho Yorkshire Cottage, where they had an oppor- tunity of seeing the other leather trades department at work.

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A LUNATIC•
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A LUNATIC•
-- Drowned in Appleton Quarry.

-- -- Mr S Brighouae, county coroner, held an inquiry last Friday ict3 the circumitancea attending the death of Margaret Kelly, wife ef John Kelly, of 2, Tarrant-street, Widnes, who committed suicide by drowning in Apple- ton Quarry, on Tuesday last. John Kelly, chemical labourer, said the deceased was his wife,and was 42 years of age. The deceased was all right until New Year's Day, when she went strange in her manner. She continued very strange, and on the 6th of Jaauary attempted to cut her throat. Police- constable Davidson arrested her, and she was brought before the magistrates on a charge of attempted suicide. She was then committed to the workhouse hospital for 14 days. At the end of that time she was discharged as being well enough. She seemed somewhat better until February, when she again attempted to take away her life. She was then sent to Rainhill Asylum. She remained a patient there until Friday last, when he received a letter from the super- intendent of the asylum asking him to bring her away. Witness went, and she was banded over to him by the nurses as being cured. Upon reaching Widnes, the de- ceased appeared to be very nervoua, and did not, ac- cording to witness's idea, seem all right. During the week-end she visited her friends. On Monday night deceased would not get in bed, and repeatedly said she was a ..dead corpse." She remairei on the bed all night. Witoess left his daughter with her in the room, and went to his work at 6 a.m. next morning. The Coroner here stated that he had written to Dr Wigglesworth, of Rainhill Asylum, and informed him of the circumstances. In reply, he said that the deceased was admitted in February, suffering from melancholia, and at that time appeared suicidal. About July she was I fully recovered, and was quite well enough to be dis- charged, but he thought it better to detain her anotber month under observation. In some instances these suicidal symptoms return instantly. Shs was discharged on Friday week as being .well enough to leave. Dr Wilson, one of the assistant medical men at the institute, corroborated.
Tne Coroner (after reviewing the evidence)said insane persons were full of deceit. They would appear cheer- ful, and yet in their own cninds phtting to take away their life.
The jury,after a short deliberation in private,returnad a verdict of " Suicide whilst of unsound wind."
